  • Internal (organic) growth: expanding by reinvesting profit, opening new outlets, developing new products.
  • External growth: joining with another firm through a merger or a takeover (one firm buys another).

Mergers

A merger is when two or more firms join together to form one firm.

Type of mergerDefinitionExampleAdvantagesDisadvantages
HorizontalFirms at the same stage of production in the same industryTwo car makers mergeEconomies of scale; higher market share; less competition; can close duplicated branchesRisk of diseconomies of scale; job losses where work is duplicated; less choice and possibly higher prices for consumers; all sales still depend on one market
Vertical backwardJoins with a firm at an earlier stage of production (a supplier)Chocolate maker merges with a cocoa farmSecure supplies; control over quality and cost of inputs; supplies can be denied to rivalsManagers have no experience of the supplier’s industry; less freedom to switch to a cheaper supplier
Vertical forwardJoins with a firm at a later stage of production (a customer or outlet)Coffee roaster merges with a chain of cafesSecure outlets for the product; keeps the retail profit; direct contact with consumersManagers have no experience of retailing; outlets may sell only the firm’s own brand, reducing choice
ConglomerateFirms in unrelated industriesFood company merges with a solar panel businessDiversification spreads risk: a fall in one market can be offset by anotherManagers lack knowledge of the new industry; few economies of scale as the products are unrelated; harder to coordinate

Why firms merge: to gain economies of scale, increase market share and market power, raise profits, spread risk and survive.

1
Chain of reasoning: horizontal mergerTwo supermarkets merge → larger scale of output.
2
Bulk-buyingPurchasing economies of scale → lower average total cost.
3
Market powerFewer competitors → greater ability to set prices.
4
OutcomeHigher profits; consumers gain only if cost savings are passed on, otherwise they face higher prices and less choice.

Economies and diseconomies of scale

Economies of scale are the reductions in average total cost (ATC), the cost per unit, as a firm increases its scale of production. Diseconomies of scale are rises in average total cost when a firm grows too large.

  • Internal economies and diseconomies come from the growth of the firm itself.
  • External economies and diseconomies come from the growth of the whole industry, usually in one area, and affect every firm in it whatever its own size.
Internal economies of scale (ATC falls as the firm grows)Internal diseconomies of scale (ATC rises as the firm grows too large)
Purchasing (bulk-buying): discounts for buying inputs in large quantitiesPoor communication: messages pass through many layers and get delayed or distorted
Technical: can afford and fully use advanced machineryWeak coordination and control: hard to manage many departments and sites
Financial: banks lend at lower interest rates to large, secure firmsLow worker motivation: workers feel unvalued, so productivity falls
Marketing: advertising cost is spread over more outputSlow decision-making: the firm reacts late to changes in the market
Managerial: can employ specialist managers
Risk-bearing: can diversify products and markets
External economies of scale (the industry grows, ATC falls for all firms in it)External diseconomies of scale (the industry grows too large, ATC rises for all firms in it)
A pool of skilled labour develops locally, cutting recruitment and training costsCompetition for workers pushes wages up
Specialist suppliers and services set up nearbyShortages push up the price of land, rents and raw materials
Better infrastructure and transport links are built for the industryTraffic congestion delays deliveries and raises transport costs
Shared research; colleges offer courses designed for the industryPollution may lead to extra costs or regulation

Drawing it: label the axes Average total cost and Output, draw a U-shaped curve labelled ATC, and mark the lowest point. To the left of the lowest point the curve slopes down (economies of scale); to the right it slopes up (diseconomies of scale).

Common Mistake
Saying economies of scale reduce total cost. Total cost rises as output rises; it is the average total cost per unit that falls.

3.5 Firms and production

Production is the process of converting factors of production (inputs) into goods and services (output).

Demand for factors of production

A firm’s demand for land, labour, capital and enterprise is a derived demand. It depends on:

  • Demand for the product: if more of the product is wanted, more factors are needed to make it.
  • The price of different factors: if wages rise compared with the price of machines, firms use more capital and less labour (where one can replace the other).
  • Their availability: a firm can only use the factors it can get. Where skilled workers are in short supply, firms may turn to machines; where land is scarce, they build upwards.
  • Their productivity: the more a factor produces for what it costs, the more of it firms want to use.

Labour-intensive and capital-intensive production

Labour-intensive production uses a high proportion of labour relative to capital (hairdressing, handmade crafts, tea picking). Capital-intensive production uses a high proportion of capital (car assembly, oil refining).

Reasons for the choice: firms choose capital-intensive methods when labour is expensive or scarce, output is large and standardised, and the technology and finance are available. Labour-intensive methods suit personal services, hand-made or customised products, small outputs and economies where wages are low.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Labour-intensiveLow start-up cost; flexible, as workers can change tasks and make customised products; personal service; workers can suggest improvements; creates jobsHigher cost per unit when output is large; quality can vary between workers; risk of strikes, absence and wage demands; costs rise if wages rise
Capital-intensiveLarge output at a low cost per unit (technical economies of scale); consistent quality; machines can run day and nightHigh cost of buying, maintaining and replacing machines; often needs borrowing; less flexible if demand or fashion changes; a breakdown can stop production; workers’ tasks may be repetitive

Production and productivity

Production
Total output of goods and services
Productivity
Output per unit of factor input per time period
Labour productivity
Total output ÷ number of workers

Productivity vs production: production is total output; productivity is how efficiently inputs are turned into output. Higher productivity lowers average costs, can raise wages and profits, and improves international competitiveness.

Worked example
A factory with 20 workers makes 400 chairs a week. It then employs 30 workers and makes 540 chairs a week.
  • Before: labour productivity = 400 ÷ 20 = 20 chairs per worker per week.
  • After: labour productivity = 540 ÷ 30 = 18 chairs per worker per week.
  • Production rose (400 to 540) but productivity fell (20 to 18).
  • Influences on production: the demand for the product, and the quantity and quality of factors of production the firm uses (more workers, machines or land raise output).
  • Influences on productivity: education and training, the amount and quality of capital, new technology, motivation and management, and division of labour.

Effects of changes in investment on productivity

Investment is spending on capital goods such as machinery, equipment, buildings and software.

  • A rise in investment gives each worker more or better equipment, so output per worker rises. For example, a bakery that replaces hand-mixing with an industrial mixer can make more loaves with the same staff. Higher productivity lowers average total cost and makes the firm more competitive.
  • The gain is not automatic. Workers may need training to use the new equipment, production may be disrupted while it is installed, and the money has an opportunity cost (and interest, if it is borrowed).
  • A fall in investment means worn-out machines are not replaced and the firm falls behind on technology, so productivity grows slowly or falls and the firm becomes less competitive.

3.6 Firms’ costs, revenue and objectives

Definitions of costs of production

Fixed cost (FC)
Does not change with output (rent, insurance)
Variable cost (VC)
Changes with output (raw materials, energy)
Total cost (TC)
TC = FC + VC
Average total cost
ATC = TC ÷ output
Average fixed cost
AFC = FC ÷ output (always falls as output rises)
Average variable cost
AVC = VC ÷ output
Total revenue (TR)
TR = price × quantity sold
Average revenue (AR)
AR = TR ÷ quantity = price
Profit
Profit = TR − TC

Two checks that are useful in calculations: ATC = AFC + AVC, and fixed costs still have to be paid when output is zero, so at zero output TC = FC.

Calculation of costs of production

Worked example
A bakery pays rent of $600 a week. Each loaf costs $0.80 in ingredients and energy and sells for $2.00. It sells 1,000 loaves.
  • VC = 1,000 × $0.80 = $800; TC = $600 + $800 = $1,400
  • ATC = $1,400 ÷ 1,000 = $1.40 per loaf; AFC = $600 ÷ 1,000 = $0.60; AVC = $800 ÷ 1,000 = $0.80
  • TR = 1,000 × $2.00 = $2,000; Profit = $2,000 − $1,400 = $600
  • If output doubles to 2,000, AFC falls to $0.30 and ATC to $1.10: fixed costs are spread over more units.

Worked table. A juice stall has fixed costs of $600 a week (rent and equipment hire). Its variable costs (fruit, bottles, casual staff) are shown in the table. Every other column is calculated from FC and VC. The figures are made up for illustration.

Output (bottles per week)FC ($)VC ($)TC ($)AFC ($)AVC ($)ATC ($)
06000600–––
2006002008003.001.004.00
4006003409401.500.852.35
6006004801,0801.000.801.80
8006007201,3200.750.901.65
1,0006001,1001,7000.601.101.70

Check one row yourself, for 800 bottles: TC = 600 + 720 = $1,320; AFC = 600 ÷ 800 = $0.75; AVC = 720 ÷ 800 = $0.90; ATC = 1,320 ÷ 800 = $1.65 (which is also 0.75 + 0.90).

Working backwards: exam questions often give you some figures and ask for a missing one. If ATC is $1.80 at 600 bottles, TC = 1.80 × 600 = $1,080. If TC is $1,080 and FC is $600, VC = 1,080 − 600 = $480.

How changes in output affect costs

  • FC is a horizontal line: it is the same at every output, including zero.
  • VC starts at the origin and rises as output rises. TC has the same shape but starts at the level of FC.
  • AFC always falls as output rises, because the same fixed cost is divided by more units.
  • ATC is usually U-shaped. It falls at first, mainly because AFC is falling, then rises when rising AVC outweighs the fall in AFC (at the stall, extra staff get in each other’s way and overtime has to be paid).

Definitions and calculation of revenue

  • Total revenue (TR) is the total amount a firm receives from selling its product: TR = price × quantity sold.
  • Average revenue (AR) is the revenue received per unit sold: AR = TR ÷ quantity sold. If every unit is sold at the same price, AR is equal to the price.
Worked example
The juice stall sells 800 bottles in a week at $2.50 each.
  • TR = $2.50 × 800 = $2,000
  • AR = $2,000 ÷ 800 = $2.50 (the price)
  • Profit = TR − TC = $2,000 − $1,320 = $680
  • Working backwards: a firm with TR of $4,500 from 1,500 units has AR = $4,500 ÷ 1,500 = $3.00.

The influence of sales on revenue

  • If the price stays the same, selling more raises TR in proportion: at $2.50 a bottle, 800 bottles bring in $2,000 and 1,000 bottles bring in $2,500. AR stays at $2.50.
  • If the firm must cut its price to sell more, AR falls, and what happens to TR depends on price elasticity of demand (see 2.6):
    • Price cut from $2.50 to $2.00 and sales rise from 1,000 to 1,400: TR rises from $2,500 to $2,800. Sales rose by 40% after a 20% price cut, so demand is price elastic.
    • Price cut from $2.50 to $2.00 and sales rise only from 1,000 to 1,100: TR falls from $2,500 to $2,200. Sales rose by 10% after a 20% price cut, so demand is price inelastic.
  • More sales do not always mean more profit: compare the extra revenue with the extra cost of producing the extra output.

Objectives of firms

  • Survival — covering costs and staying in business; the main aim for new firms and in a recession.
  • Social welfare — acting in the interests of society rather than for profit alone, e.g. public-sector firms providing an affordable service, charities and social enterprises, or private firms cutting carbon emissions and sourcing ethically.
  • Profit maximisation — making the largest possible gap between TR and TC; the traditional aim of private-sector firms. Profit rewards owners and funds investment.
  • Growth — increasing the size of the firm (output, sales or market share). Larger size brings economies of scale, market power and security.

Objectives can change over time and can conflict: a firm that cuts prices to grow gives up some profit now in the hope of more later.

Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but you may see sales revenue maximisation mentioned as a further objective, sometimes preferred by managers whose pay is linked to sales.

3.7 Types of markets

Markets differ in how many firms compete in them. (Older papers call this topic “market structure”.) You need two types: competitive markets and monopoly markets. No diagrams are needed for either.

Competitive markets

A competitive market has a high number of firms competing to sell to the same customers.

  • Characteristics: many firms, each with a small market share; low barriers to entry and exit, so new firms can join easily; similar products; each firm has little or no power over the market price.
  • Advantages: low prices; firms must keep costs down and use resources efficiently; pressure to improve quality and bring out new products; wide choice; firms respond quickly to what consumers want.
  • Disadvantages: firms may be too small to gain economies of scale; low profit leaves little to spend on research and development; some firms may cut quality or wages to keep prices down; firms that cannot compete close, causing job losses.

Monopoly markets

A monopoly is a market with only one firm selling the product. (In practice the term is also used for one firm that dominates a market.)

  • Characteristics: one seller, so the firm is the industry; high barriers to entry (legal barriers such as patents and licences, large economies of scale, control of a key resource, high start-up costs, brand loyalty); a product with no close substitutes; the firm is a price-maker (it can choose its price, but then consumers decide how much to buy).
Advantages of monopolyDisadvantages of monopoly
Economies of scale can mean lower costs and possibly lower pricesHigher prices and lower output than in a competitive market
High profits can fund research and development and innovationLess choice for consumers
Avoids wasteful duplication (natural monopoly, e.g. water pipes)Less incentive to be efficient or improve quality
Stable, can invest long-termMay exploit suppliers and workers

Effect of the number of firms on price, quality, choice and profit

High number of firms (competitive market)Only one firm (monopoly market)
PriceLow: a firm that charges more than its rivals loses customersLikely to be higher, as consumers have no alternative; could be lower if large economies of scale are passed on
QualityLikely to be high: firms improve quality to attract customersMay be lower, as there is no rival to lose customers to; may be higher if profits are spent on research and development
ChoiceWide: many sellers and many versions of the productLimited: one seller, though it may offer a range of its own products
ProfitLow for each firm: high profits attract new firms, which raises supply and pushes price and profit downCan stay high for a long time, because barriers to entry keep new firms out
Model answer
Explain why a surgeon usually earns more than a shop assistant. [4]
A surgeon needs many years of training and high qualifications, so few people are able to enter the occupation and the supply of surgeons is low. The demand for surgeons is high because their skills are essential and their productivity (value of output) is great. High demand and low supply result in a high equilibrium wage. In contrast, shop assistant work requires little training, so supply is large, and each assistant can be replaced easily, so the equilibrium wage is lower.
Examiner Tip
In “Discuss” questions about mergers, a national minimum wage or monopoly, always give both sides and a justified conclusion that depends on conditions (e.g. “a merger benefits consumers only if the savings from economies of scale are passed on as lower prices and competition authorities prevent abuse of market power”).
Common Mistake
Confusing productivity with production. A firm can produce more simply by hiring more workers while productivity (output per worker) stays the same or falls.

Quick Checklist

  • 3.1 I can describe the forms, functions and characteristics of money and explain the role and importance of central banks and commercial banks.
  • 3.2 I can explain how income, the rate of interest, confidence, age and culture affect households’ spending, saving and borrowing.
  • 3.3 I can draw labour market diagrams for a change in demand or supply and for a national minimum wage, explain how trade union bargaining power and government policy affect wages, and give reasons for differences in wages.
  • 3.3 I can explain the causes and consequences of changes in occupational and geographical mobility of labour, and the advantages and disadvantages of division of labour.
  • 3.4 I can classify firms, compare small and large firms, and give the advantages and disadvantages of horizontal, vertical and conglomerate mergers.
  • 3.4 I can explain internal and external economies and diseconomies of scale and show them on an ATC diagram.
  • 3.5 I can explain what influences the demand for factors of production, compare labour-intensive and capital-intensive production, distinguish production from productivity and explain how investment affects productivity.
  • 3.6 I can define and calculate TC, ATC, FC, AFC, VC, AVC, TR and AR, draw diagrams showing how costs change with output, and explain the four objectives of firms.
  • 3.7 I can describe the characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of competitive markets and monopoly markets and their effects on price, quality, choice and profit.
Topic 4 · Government and the Macroeconomy

Government and the Macroeconomy

This topic covers what governments try to achieve for the whole economy (4.1), the three types of policy they use: fiscal (4.2), monetary (4.3) and supply-side (4.4), and how economic growth (4.5), unemployment (4.6) and inflation (4.7) are measured, what causes them and what they lead to. Expect calculations using budget, real GDP, unemployment and CPI figures, and 8-mark “Discuss” questions on which policy works best.

4.1 Government macroeconomic intervention

Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole: total output, total employment and the general price level. Governments intervene because markets left alone do not always deliver steady growth, jobs for everyone who wants one, or stable prices.

The six macroeconomic aims

Economic growth
A rise in real GDP over time
Full employment / low unemployment
Almost everyone willing and able to work has a job
Stable prices / low inflation
The general price level rises slowly and predictably
Balance of payments stability
Avoid large, persistent current account deficits or surpluses
Redistribution of income
Reduce the gap between high and low incomes
Environmental sustainability
Meet present needs without damaging future generations’ ability to meet theirs

Why governments choose these aims, and the criteria they may set

A criterion is the measure a government uses to judge whether an aim has been met. Many governments turn an aim into a target figure. The figures below are illustrations of the kind of target used, not rules: each government sets its own.

AimReason for choosing itCriterion a government may set
Economic growthMore output means higher incomes, more jobs and more tax revenue to spend on public servicesA target rate of growth of real GDP, e.g. 3% a year, without a recession
Full employment / low unemploymentUnemployment wastes labour, lowers living standards and costs the government benefits and lost taxAn unemployment rate kept below a stated level, e.g. under 4% of the labour force
Stable prices / low inflationProtects the purchasing power of incomes and savings; firms can plan and invest; exports stay price competitiveAn inflation target for the central bank, e.g. a rise in the CPI of about 2% a year
Balance of payments stabilityA country that keeps spending more abroad than it earns has to borrow or run down its reserves of foreign currencyA current account close to balance over a period of years, or a deficit below a set percentage of GDP
Redistribution of incomeReduces poverty and gives people a fairer chance; very unequal incomes can cause social tensionA fall in the percentage of households below the poverty line, or a narrower gap between the richest and poorest groups
Environmental sustainabilityPollution, climate change and running out of resources threaten future output and healthA target to cut carbon emissions by a set date, or a target share of electricity from renewable sources

Governments rarely treat all six as equally urgent. The priority depends on the problem of the moment: a country with 12% inflation will put stable prices first, while one in a recession will put growth and jobs first.

Possible conflicts between aims

A conflict means that a policy which moves the economy towards one aim moves it away from another. The syllabus names three:

  • Full employment and stable prices: as unemployment falls, more people earn and spend, so total demand rises and may cause demand-pull inflation. Firms also find it harder to recruit, so they offer higher wages, which raises costs and prices.
  • Economic growth and environmental sustainability: producing more usually uses more energy and raw materials and creates more waste, so carbon emissions, pollution and resource depletion rise.
  • Full employment and balance of payments stability: when more people are in work, incomes are higher and households buy more imports (and firms import more raw materials). Goods that could have been exported may be sold at home instead. The current account moves towards deficit.

Other conflicts you could mention: fast growth in total demand can cause inflation, and very high taxes used to redistribute income may weaken incentives to work and invest, slowing growth.

Examiner Tip
Conflicts are possible, not certain. Supply-side policy can raise growth and employment while holding prices down, and investment in green technology can support both growth and sustainability. Saying this earns evaluation marks.

The role of government Background

Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but it appeared in older past papers. Governments act locally (refuse collection, local roads), nationally (defence, education, healthcare, benefits, regulation, managing the macroeconomy) and internationally (trade agreements, cooperation on climate change). A government is also a producer, through state-owned enterprises, and an employer.

4.2 Fiscal policy

The government budget

  • Government budget: a statement of the government’s planned spending and planned revenue (mainly from taxes) for the year ahead.
  • Government budget deficit: government spending is greater than government revenue. The gap is covered by borrowing, which adds to the national debt.
  • Government budget surplus: government revenue is greater than government spending. The surplus can be used to repay past borrowing.
  • A balanced budget means the two are equal.
Budget balance
Government revenue − government spending (negative = deficit, positive = surplus)
Worked example · budget deficit and surplus

Country X (illustrative figures): tax revenue $385 billion, government spending $420 billion.
Budget balance = 385 − 420 = −$35 billion, so there is a budget deficit of $35 billion.
If GDP is $700 billion, the deficit is 35 ÷ 700 × 100 = 5% of GDP.

Country Y: government revenue $510 billion, government spending $495 billion.
Budget balance = 510 − 495 = +$15 billion, a budget surplus of $15 billion.

Common Mistake
Confusing a budget deficit with the national debt. The deficit is the shortfall in one year; the national debt is the total the government owes from all past borrowing. Also give the answer with its sign in words (“a deficit of $35 billion”) and its units.

Reasons for government spending

Area of spendingReasonEffect
EducationA merit good that would be under-consumed if left to the marketMore skilled, more productive workers; higher future incomes and growth
HealthcareA merit good; many could not afford treatmentHealthier workforce, fewer days lost to illness, longer life expectancy
Defence, police and justicePublic goods that private firms would not provideSecurity and safe conditions for households and firms
Infrastructure (roads, rail, power, broadband)Too costly or too risky for private firms aloneLower transport and production costs for firms; attracts investment
Welfare benefits and state pensionsTo support people on low incomes, the unemployed and the elderlyLess poverty and inequality; keeps consumer spending going in a downturn
Environmental protectionTo reduce external costs and protect resourcesLess pollution; supports environmental sustainability
Interest on the national debtPast borrowing must be servicedMoney that cannot be used for other services (an opportunity cost)

Government spending is also used to influence total demand: raising it to boost output and jobs, cutting it to reduce inflation. Every area of spending has an opportunity cost, because the money could have been spent elsewhere or left with taxpayers.

Reasons for taxation

The syllabus lists six:

  • Raising revenue to pay for government spending.
  • Discouraging consumption of demerit goods: taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks raise their prices.
  • Reducing imports: a tariff (a tax on imports) makes foreign goods dearer, so consumers switch to home-produced goods.
  • Redistributing income: progressive taxes take proportionately more from high earners, and the revenue funds benefits and services for those on low incomes.
  • Influencing total demand: higher taxes reduce spending and inflation; lower taxes raise spending, output and employment.
  • Encouraging environmental sustainability: carbon taxes, fuel duty and landfill taxes make polluters pay for the external costs they create.

Classification of taxes

TypeMeaningExample
DirectTax on income or wealth, paid to the government by the person or firm taxedIncome tax, corporation tax (on firms’ profits), inheritance tax
IndirectTax on spending; collected by sellers and usually passed on to buyers in higher pricesSales tax / VAT / GST, excise duty, tariffs
ProgressiveTakes a larger percentage of income as income risesIncome tax with rising bands (e.g. 10%, then 20%, then 30%)
RegressiveTakes a larger percentage of income from those on low incomes than from those on high incomesMost indirect taxes, e.g. a fixed excise duty per litre of fuel
ProportionalTakes the same percentage of income at all income levelsA flat-rate income tax of 15%
Worked example · why an indirect tax can be regressive

Two people each pay $300 a year in tax on the fuel they buy. Asha earns $10 000 a year: 300 ÷ 10 000 × 100 = 3% of her income. Ben earns $60 000: 300 ÷ 60 000 × 100 = 0.5% of his income. The amount is the same, but the percentage of income is higher for the lower earner, so the tax is regressive.

Common Mistake
Defining a progressive tax as one where “the rich pay more”. Under a proportional tax the rich also pay a larger amount. A progressive tax takes a higher proportion (percentage) of income as income rises.

Impact of taxation

  • Consumers: direct taxes cut disposable income; indirect taxes raise prices. Both reduce purchasing power, and indirect taxes change what people buy (less of the taxed product).
  • Workers: higher income tax lowers take-home pay and may weaken the incentive to work extra hours, seek promotion or enter the labour force.
  • Producers/firms: corporation tax reduces profit after tax, leaving less to invest; indirect taxes raise costs and may reduce sales; higher income tax on customers lowers demand.
  • The government: tax is its main source of revenue. A higher tax rate usually raises more, but not if it sharply reduces work, sales or encourages tax avoidance.
  • The economy: higher taxes reduce total demand, which may slow growth and raise unemployment but lower inflation and imports. Progressive taxes reduce inequality; environmental taxes reduce pollution.

Qualities of a good tax Background

Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but useful for evaluating a tax. A good tax is equitable (based on ability to pay), certain (people know how much and when to pay), convenient to pay, economical to collect, flexible, and does not badly damage incentives to work, save or invest.

Definition of fiscal policy and its measures

Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxation to influence total demand (aggregate demand) and so the level of economic activity. The two measures are changes in taxes and changes in government spending.

Expansionary fiscal policyContractionary fiscal policy
MeasuresRaise government spending and/or cut taxesCut government spending and/or raise taxes
Effect on the budgetMoves towards a deficit (or a larger one)Moves towards a surplus (or a smaller deficit)
AimIncrease total demand: boost growth, cut unemploymentReduce total demand: control inflation, reduce spending on imports
DrawbacksInflation, more government borrowing, more imports, time lagsSlower growth, higher unemployment, fewer public services

Effects of fiscal policy on the macroeconomic aims

AimHow fiscal policy can help
Economic growthLower income tax raises disposable income and consumer spending; more government spending adds directly to total demand, so firms raise output. Spending on education and infrastructure also raises productive capacity.
Full employmentHigher total demand means firms need more workers (demand for labour is derived from demand for products), so cyclical unemployment falls.
Stable pricesHigher taxes or lower government spending reduce total demand, easing demand-pull inflation.
Balance of payments stabilityHigher income tax reduces spending, including spending on imports; tariffs make imports dearer.
Redistribution of incomeMore progressive taxes, with the revenue spent on benefits, state education and healthcare for low-income households.
Environmental sustainabilityTaxes on carbon and pollution; subsidies and government spending on renewable energy and public transport.

Limits: tax and spending changes take time to agree and to work; people may save a tax cut instead of spending it if confidence is low; expansionary policy increases government borrowing; and helping one aim may harm another (see the conflicts in 4.1).

4.3 Monetary policy

Definitions

  • Money supply: the total amount of money in an economy, made up of notes and coins in circulation plus the deposits held in bank accounts.
  • Monetary policy: decisions, usually taken by the central bank, on the interest rate, the money supply and the foreign exchange rate, made in order to influence total demand.

Monetary policy measures

  • Changes in the interest rate: the central bank sets a key rate, and commercial banks change the rates they charge borrowers and pay savers in line with it.
  • Changes in the money supply: the central bank can make it easier or harder for commercial banks to lend, or create new money and use it to buy government bonds from banks, giving them more funds to lend.
  • Changes in the foreign exchange rate: the central bank can buy or sell its own currency, or change the interest rate, to move the currency’s value. A lower exchange rate makes exports cheaper and imports dearer; a higher one does the opposite.
1
Chain of reasoning: interest rate riseCentral bank raises the interest rate.
2
Borrowing costs riseLoans and mortgages become more expensive; saving is more rewarding.
3
Spending fallsHouseholds cut consumption; firms cut investment. The currency may rise in value, reducing demand for exports.
4
OutcomeTotal demand falls → demand-pull inflation slows, but growth may slow and unemployment may rise.
  • Expansionary monetary policy: cut the interest rate, increase the money supply, lower the foreign exchange rate.
  • Contractionary monetary policy: raise the interest rate, reduce the money supply, raise the foreign exchange rate.

Effect of monetary policy on the macroeconomic aims

AimHow monetary policy can help
Economic growthA lower interest rate makes borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding, so consumption and investment rise and firms increase output. More investment also adds to productive capacity.
Full employmentHigher spending means firms take on more workers. A lower exchange rate raises demand for exports, creating jobs in export industries.
Stable pricesA higher interest rate or a smaller money supply reduces spending and demand-pull inflation. A higher exchange rate makes imported goods and raw materials cheaper, reducing cost-push inflation.
Balance of payments stabilityA lower exchange rate makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, which can reduce a current account deficit. A higher interest rate reduces spending on imports.

Monetary policy is a blunt tool for the other two aims: an interest rate change cannot be aimed at low-income households or at polluters, although lower rates do make it cheaper to borrow for green investment.

Limits: it can take a year or more for an interest rate change to have its full effect; if confidence is low, households and firms may not borrow even when rates are cut; the rate cannot be cut far below zero; a higher rate hurts borrowers and discourages investment, which harms long-run growth.

4.4 Supply-side policy

Supply-side policy is government action to increase the economy’s productive capacity (its total supply) by raising the quantity and quality of resources and making markets work more efficiently. On a PPC diagram, successful supply-side policy shifts the curve outwards.

Supply-side policy measures

MeasureHow it worksPossible drawback
Education and trainingRaises workers’ skills, productivity and occupational mobilityCostly; results take years to appear
Infrastructure spendingBetter transport, power and broadband cut firms’ costs and delivery timesVery expensive; projects may run late; building can harm the environment
Labour market reformsMaking it easier to hire, reducing trade union power, or reforming benefits so that work pays more than staying unemployedLess job security and lower incomes for some workers; more inequality
Lower direct taxesLower income tax rewards work; lower corporation tax leaves firms more profit to investLess tax revenue; people may choose more leisure, not more work
DeregulationRemoving rules that restrict firms lowers costs and lets new firms enter, increasing competitionWeaker protection for consumers, workers or the environment
Improving incentives to work and investTax relief or grants for firms that buy capital goods or carry out research; help with childcare so that more parents can workCost to the government; some firms would have invested anyway
PrivatisationSelling state-owned enterprises to the private sector; the profit motive pushes firms to cut costs and improve qualityMay create a private monopoly that raises prices; jobs may be cut

You may also mention better healthcare (a healthier workforce is more productive), which works in the same way as education and training.

Effects of supply-side policy on the macroeconomic aims

  • Economic growth: more and better resources raise productive capacity, allowing output to keep rising in the long run.
  • Full employment: training and better job information reduce structural and frictional unemployment; stronger incentives bring more people into work.
  • Stable prices: higher productivity lowers firms’ costs, and more competition holds prices down, so growth can happen without inflation.
  • Balance of payments stability: lower costs and better quality make exports more competitive and home-produced goods more attractive than imports.
  • Redistribution of income: education and training can raise the earnings of low-paid workers, but lower direct taxes and benefit reforms may widen the gap.
  • Environmental sustainability: investment in renewable energy and clean technology helps; deregulation may harm it.

Evaluation: supply-side policy is the only type that can raise growth and employment while lowering inflation, so it avoids some conflicts between aims. But it is costly, takes a long time to work, has uncertain results, and does little if the problem is a lack of total demand, since extra capacity is no use if nobody is buying.

4.5 Economic growth

Definition and measurement

  • Economic growth is an increase in the real output of an economy over time.
  • Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of the goods and services produced in a country in a given period, usually a year.
  • Real GDP is GDP adjusted for inflation, so it changes only when the volume of output changes. Growth is measured by the percentage change in real GDP. (Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, so it can rise just because prices rose.)
  • Real GDP per head (real GDP ÷ population) is used to compare living standards: see Topic 5.
Economic growth rate
(Real GDP this year − real GDP last year) ÷ real GDP last year × 100
Worked example · growth rate

Country X’s real GDP rises from $500 billion to $515 billion. Growth rate = (515 − 500) ÷ 500 × 100 = 15 ÷ 500 × 100 = 3%.

Why “real” matters: if nominal GDP rose by 6% in a year when prices rose by 4%, output itself grew by only about 2%.

Causes of economic growth

  • An increase in total demand: more consumer spending, investment, government spending or net exports. Firms respond by using spare capacity and unemployed workers to produce more (a movement from inside the PPC towards the curve).
  • An increase in the quantity of resources: a larger labour force (immigration, a higher retirement age, more women working), more capital goods from investment, newly discovered natural resources.
  • An increase in the quality of resources: better education, training and healthcare raise labour productivity; new technology makes capital more productive.

More or better resources shift the PPC outwards, so the economy can produce more. Demand must also rise for that extra capacity to be used.

Consequences of economic growth

Advantages of economic growthDisadvantages of economic growth
Higher incomes and living standardsPollution, carbon emissions and resource depletion
Lower unemployment as firms need more workersMay cause inflation if total demand grows faster than capacity
More tax revenue for public services, without raising tax ratesBenefits may be unevenly spread, widening inequality
Firms earn more profit and invest moreHigher incomes may pull in more imports; longer working hours, stress and congestion

Recession: definition and causes

A recession is a fall in real GDP for two consecutive quarters (six months) or more.

  • A decrease in total demand: a fall in consumer or business confidence, a rise in interest rates or taxes, cuts in government spending, a banking crisis, or a downturn abroad that reduces exports.
  • A decrease in the quantity of resources: net emigration of workers, natural disasters or war destroying capital, natural resources running out.
  • A decrease in the quality of resources: a serious outbreak of disease lowering workers’ health and productivity, skills lost during long periods of unemployment, capital wearing out because firms stop replacing it.

Consequences of recession

GroupConsequences of a recession
ConsumersLower incomes and less confidence, so they buy fewer goods and services, switch to cheaper products and save more “just in case”. Living standards fall. Prices may rise more slowly, which helps those whose incomes have not fallen.
WorkersJob losses, shorter hours and less overtime; pay rises are smaller because workers have less bargaining power; it is harder for school leavers and the unemployed to find work.
Producers/firmsLower sales revenue and profit; investment is cut; some firms close. Firms selling low-priced basics may see demand rise, and surviving firms find it easier to recruit.
The governmentLess revenue from income tax, sales taxes and corporation tax, and more spending on unemployment benefits, so the budget moves towards a deficit (or a larger one). Pressure to act to raise total demand.

Policies to promote economic growth and their effectiveness

PolicyHow it promotes growthHow effective?
Expansionary fiscal policyLower taxes and higher government spending raise total demand, so firms produce moreWorks when there is spare capacity. Near full capacity it causes inflation instead. Adds to government borrowing; a tax cut may be saved, not spent.
Expansionary monetary policyLower interest rate raises consumption and investment; a lower exchange rate raises net exportsSlow to take effect; weak if confidence is low; may raise inflation and household debt.
Supply-side policyRaises the quantity and quality of resources, increasing productive capacityThe only way to keep growth going in the long run, and without inflation, but slow, costly and uncertain.

The best results usually come from a mix: demand-side policy to use existing capacity now, and supply-side policy to expand capacity for the future. Many governments also aim for growth that is environmentally sustainable, for example by investing in renewable energy.

4.6 Employment and unemployment

Definitions

  • Employment: people who have a paid job, working for an employer or for themselves.
  • Unemployment: people of working age who are willing and able to work and are actively looking for a job, but do not have one.
  • Full employment: the lowest level of unemployment that can realistically be reached. It is not zero, because there will always be some people between jobs.
  • The labour force is the employed plus the unemployed. Students, full-time carers, retired people and others who are not looking for work are outside the labour force, so they are not counted as unemployed.

Measurement of unemployment

Unemployment is measured with a labour force survey. A large sample of households is interviewed at regular intervals and asked whether each adult has a job and, if not, whether they have recently looked for work and are available to start. The results are scaled up to estimate the figure for the whole country.

  • Strengths: it counts everyone who is looking for work, whether or not they claim benefits, and it uses an internationally agreed definition, so countries can be compared.
  • Weaknesses: it is an estimate from a sample, so there is some sampling error; it is costly and takes time to collect; it does not show people who have given up looking, or part-time workers who want more hours.
Unemployment rate
Number of unemployed ÷ labour force × 100
Labour force
Employed + unemployed
Worked example · unemployment rate

Country X has a population of 20 million, of whom 9.2 million are employed and 0.8 million are unemployed.
Labour force = 9.2 + 0.8 = 10 million. Unemployment rate = 0.8 ÷ 10 × 100 = 8%.

Common Mistake
Dividing by the population (0.8 ÷ 20 gives 4%) or by the number employed. The unemployment rate is always a percentage of the labour force.
Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but older past papers also mention the claimant count, which simply counts the people receiving unemployment benefits. It is cheap and quick but leaves out unemployed people who do not, or cannot, claim.

Causes/types of unemployment

TypeCauseExampleSuitable policy
FrictionalShort-term: workers are between jobs or looking for their first oneA graduate searching for a first jobBetter job information, job centres, online vacancy sites
StructuralA long-term change in the structure of the economy: an industry declines or new technology replaces workers, and their skills (or location) do not match the new jobsCoal miners after mines close; cashiers replaced by self-checkout machinesRetraining, help with moving, incentives for firms to set up in the area
CyclicalA fall in total demand during a recession, so firms across the economy need fewer workersConstruction workers laid off in a downturnExpansionary fiscal and monetary policy
SeasonalDemand for labour varies with the time of yearBeach resort staff in the monsoon season; fruit pickers after harvestEncourage year-round activities; training for a second occupation

Consequences of unemployment

  • The individual: loss of income and lower living standards; skills and confidence fade the longer the person is out of work; stress and poorer health.
  • Producers/firms: unemployed people spend less, so sales fall. On the other hand there are more applicants for each vacancy and less pressure to raise wages.
  • The government: less revenue from income tax and sales taxes, and more spending on benefits, so the budget moves towards a deficit. Money spent on benefits has an opportunity cost.
  • The economy: output is below its potential (a point inside the PPC), so resources are wasted; inequality and poverty may rise, and crime may increase. Inflation is likely to be lower because demand is weak.

Policies to reduce unemployment and their effectiveness

PolicyHow it reduces unemploymentHow effective?
Expansionary fiscal policyTax cuts and government spending raise total demand; firms hire to meet it. The government can also create jobs directly, e.g. on building projects.Good for cyclical unemployment. Does not give workers the skills that structural unemployment requires. Risks inflation, more imports and a larger budget deficit.
Expansionary monetary policyLower interest rate raises spending and investment; a lower exchange rate raises demand for exportsGood for cyclical unemployment, but slow, and weak when confidence is low.
Supply-side policyTraining and education fix skills mismatches; better job information shortens job search; benefit and tax reforms raise the incentive to workBest for structural and frictional unemployment. Slow and costly; cannot help if there are simply too few vacancies.
Model answer
Explain how a cut in income tax might reduce unemployment. [4]
A cut in income tax increases households’ disposable income. With more disposable income, consumers spend more on goods and services, increasing total demand. Firms respond to higher demand by increasing output, and because demand for labour is derived from demand for products they need to hire more workers. This reduces cyclical unemployment. A lower tax rate may also increase the incentive to work, encouraging people to take up jobs.
Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but older papers asked about changing patterns of employment: as economies develop, jobs move from the primary and secondary sectors to the tertiary sector, more women work, and part-time, self-employed and remote work become more common.

4.7 Inflation

Definitions

  • Inflation: a sustained rise in the general price level over time. Each unit of money buys less, so the purchasing power of money falls.
  • Deflation: a sustained fall in the general price level.
Common Mistake
Thinking that a fall in the inflation rate means prices are falling. If inflation falls from 6% to 3%, prices are still rising, just more slowly. Only negative inflation (deflation) means the price level is falling.

Measurement of inflation: the Consumer Prices Index (CPI)

The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) tracks the average price of a “basket” of goods and services bought by a typical household. The inflation rate is the percentage change in the CPI over a year.

1
Choose a base yearThe index is set at 100 in that year.
2
Survey household spendingFinds what a typical household buys: the “basket” of goods and services.
3
Weight each itemBy its share of household spending (food counts for more than cinema tickets).
4
Record pricesCollect prices regularly from many shops, websites and regions.
5
Calculate the indexMultiply each item’s price index by its weight, add the results and divide by the total of the weights.
Inflation rate
(CPI this year − CPI last year) ÷ CPI last year × 100
Example
CPI 120 → 126: (6 ÷ 120) × 100 = 5%
Worked example · a weighted price index
CategoryWeightPrice index this year (base year = 100)Weight × index
Food401104400
Housing351043640
Transport251082700
Total10010 740

CPI = 10 740 ÷ 100 = 107.4, so prices have risen by 7.4% on average since the base year. Food pushed the index up most because it had both the biggest price rise and the biggest weight.

Causes of inflation

  • Demand-pull inflation: total demand grows faster than the economy can increase output, so firms raise prices. Possible triggers: tax cuts, a lower interest rate, a rise in the money supply, rising confidence, higher government spending, a boom in exports.
  • Cost-push inflation: costs of production rise and firms pass them on in higher prices to protect their profit. Possible triggers: wage rises not matched by productivity, dearer raw materials or energy, a fall in the foreign exchange rate making imports dearer, higher indirect taxes.

Consequences of inflation

GroupHow inflation affects them
SaversLose if the interest rate on their savings is below the inflation rate: the money in the account buys less than before.
LendersLose if inflation is higher than the interest rate they charge: the money repaid to them has less purchasing power than the money they lent.
BorrowersGain: the real value of what they owe falls, and if their incomes rise with inflation the debt becomes easier to repay.
ConsumersPurchasing power falls unless incomes rise as fast as prices. People on fixed incomes are hit hardest. Time is spent searching for the best prices.
WorkersReal wages fall if pay rises by less than inflation. Workers with strong bargaining power (e.g. trade union members) can protect themselves; others cannot.
Producers/firmsCosts rise; price lists must be changed often (menu costs); future costs and revenues are harder to predict, which discourages investment. Firms may gain for a while if prices rise faster than wages.
The economyExports become less price competitive and imports more attractive, so the current account may worsen. Uncertainty can slow growth. Very high inflation destroys confidence in money. People may be pushed into higher tax bands as their money incomes rise.
Worked example · a saver and inflation

Mei saves $1000 for a year at 3% interest and ends with $1030. Over the same year prices rise by 5%, so a basket that cost $1000 now costs $1050. Her savings have grown in money terms but buy less: the real return is roughly 3% − 5% = −2%. The bank that paid her, like any borrower, has gained.

How serious the effects are depends on the rate of inflation, whether it was expected (so wages and interest rates could adjust), and how it compares with inflation in other countries.

Policies to control inflation and their effectiveness

PolicyHow it controls inflationHow effective?
Contractionary monetary policyA higher interest rate or smaller money supply cuts borrowing and spending. A higher exchange rate makes imports cheaper.The main tool against demand-pull inflation. Takes time; slows growth and raises unemployment; a higher exchange rate hurts exporters.
Contractionary fiscal policyHigher income tax or lower government spending reduces total demandWorks on demand-pull inflation but is unpopular and slow to agree. Raising indirect taxes pushes prices up, not down.
Supply-side policyHigher productivity and more competition lower firms’ costs and increase capacityThe best long-run answer to cost-push inflation, but it takes years.
Examiner Tip
Always match the policy to the cause. A higher interest rate suits demand-pull inflation, but if inflation is cost-push (say, dearer imported oil) it cuts output and jobs without removing the cause. Retraining solves structural, not cyclical, unemployment. Naming the type or cause first makes your evaluation precise.
Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus (only the definition of deflation is), but older papers asked about its causes and effects. Deflation can come from falling total demand or from falling costs as productivity improves. When demand is the cause, consumers delay purchases in the hope of lower prices, firms cut output and jobs, and the real value of debts rises. Disinflation means the inflation rate is falling but still positive.
Budget balance
Government revenue − government spending
Growth rate
% change in real GDP
Recession
Real GDP falls for two consecutive quarters
Unemployment rate
Unemployed ÷ labour force × 100
Inflation rate
% change in the CPI
Three policy types
Fiscal, monetary, supply-side

Quick Checklist

  • 4.1: I can list the six macroeconomic aims, give a reason and a possible criterion for each, and explain the three named conflicts between them.
  • 4.2: I can define the government budget, calculate a budget deficit or surplus, and explain the main areas of government spending.
  • 4.2: I can give the six reasons for taxation, classify taxes (direct/indirect; progressive/regressive/proportional) and explain their impact on consumers, workers, producers/firms, the government and the economy.
  • 4.2: I can define fiscal policy and explain how changes in taxes and government spending help achieve each aim.
  • 4.3: I can define money supply and monetary policy and explain how changes in the interest rate, money supply and foreign exchange rate affect the aims.
  • 4.4: I can define supply-side policy, describe the seven measures and judge how they affect the aims.
  • 4.5: I can define economic growth and recession, calculate a growth rate from real GDP, and explain the causes and consequences of both.
  • 4.6: I can define employment, unemployment and full employment, describe the labour force survey, calculate the unemployment rate and explain the four types.
  • 4.7: I can define inflation and deflation, explain how the CPI measures inflation, and distinguish demand-pull from cost-push inflation.
  • 4.7: I can explain how inflation affects savers, lenders, borrowers, consumers, workers, producers/firms and the economy.
  • 4.5–4.7: I can discuss the range of policies for growth, unemployment and inflation and how effective each is likely to be.
Topic 5 · Economic Development

Economic Development

Four sub-topics: 5.1 Living standards (how we measure and compare them), 5.2 Poverty (what it is, why it exists and how it can be reduced), 5.3 Population (why populations change and what follows) and 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries. Paper 2 often asks you to use data on real GDP per head, HDI or population to compare two countries, so precise definitions and clear chains of reasoning are essential.

5.1 Living standards

Living standards describe the quality of life and material well-being of people in a country. Economic development is a broader idea than economic growth: it means an improvement in people’s welfare, including income, health, education and freedom of choice.

The syllabus names two indicators of living standards: real GDP per head and the Human Development Index (HDI). You need to know what each one measures and the advantages and disadvantages of each.

Real GDP per head

  • Real GDP per head (per capita) = real GDP ÷ population. It shows the average output (and income) per person, adjusted for inflation.
  • “Real” removes the effect of price changes, so a rise shows more goods and services, not just higher prices.
  • “Per head” allows for population size, so a large country is not automatically ranked above a small one.
Real GDP per head
Real GDP ÷ population
Rise in real GDP per head
Real GDP grows faster than population
Fall in real GDP per head
Population grows faster than real GDP
Worked example (illustrative figures)
Country A has a real GDP of $240 billion and a population of 30 million.
Real GDP per head = $240,000 million ÷ 30 million = $8,000.
Next year real GDP rises by 3% to $247.2 billion, but the population rises by 5% to 31.5 million.
Real GDP per head = $247,200 million ÷ 31.5 million = $7,848 (to the nearest dollar), a fall of about 1.9%. The economy grew, yet the average person is worse off because population grew faster than output.

Advantages of real GDP per head as an indicator

  • Simple and widely available: almost every country measures GDP and population, so figures are easy to find and to compare over time.
  • Adjusted for inflation and population: it shows the real quantity of goods and services available to the average person.
  • Income matters: higher average income usually means people can afford more and better food, housing, healthcare and education, so it is a reasonable guide to material living standards.
  • Objective: it is a single figure in money terms, not an opinion about what a good life is.

Disadvantages of real GDP per head as an indicator

  • It is an average — it hides the distribution of income. A few very rich people can raise the average while most people remain poor.
  • Informal (hidden) economy — unrecorded activity (cash-in-hand work, illegal trade) is excluded, so GDP may understate true output, especially in low-income countries.
  • Non-marketed output — subsistence farming, housework and voluntary work are not counted.
  • Quality of life factors are ignored — working hours, leisure time, pollution, crime, political freedom and stress.
  • Environmental damage — output from deforestation or heavy CO2 emissions raises GDP but reduces sustainability and future welfare.
  • Composition of output — high spending on defence adds to GDP but may not improve living standards as much as spending on schools or hospitals.
  • International comparisons — figures must be converted into one currency; foreign exchange rates may not reflect differences in the cost of living.

The Human Development Index (HDI) and its components

The HDI is a composite measure of living standards published by the United Nations. It combines three components into a single value between 0 and 1 (closer to 1 = more developed).

ComponentIndicator usedWhy it matters
A long and healthy lifeLife expectancy at birthReflects healthcare, nutrition, sanitation and clean water
Knowledge (education)Mean years of schooling (adults) and expected years of schooling (children)Education raises skills, productivity and life choices
A decent standard of livingGross national income (GNI) per head, adjusted for purchasing powerReflects material income and ability to buy goods and services
Health (life expectancy)Education (years of schooling)Income (GNI per head)

Advantages of HDI as an indicator

  • Broader than real GDP per head: it includes health and education, not just income.
  • Income is adjusted for differences in the cost of living (purchasing power).
  • One figure between 0 and 1 makes it easy to rank countries and to track one country’s progress over time.
  • It shows whether higher income is actually being turned into longer lives and better education.

Disadvantages of HDI as an indicator

  • Still uses averages, so it ignores inequality between groups, regions and genders.
  • Leaves out many aspects of well-being: environmental quality, political freedom, crime, working conditions, housing.
  • Years of schooling measure quantity, not the quality of education.
  • Data in low-income countries may be inaccurate or out of date.
  • Two countries can have the same HDI with very different mixes of income, health and education.

Comparing living standards and income distribution

Income distribution is how a country’s total income is shared out among its households. It is uneven (unequal) when a small share of households receives a large share of total income. Living standards and income distribution differ both within a country and between countries.

Reasons for differences within a countryReasons for differences between countries
Wages: skilled and well-qualified workers, and those in high-demand occupations, earn far more than unskilled workersProductivity: countries with more capital, better technology and more skilled workers produce more per worker, so average incomes are higher
Employment: households with no one in work depend on state benefits or familyEducation and healthcare: a healthy, educated population earns more and lives longer
Region: cities usually offer more jobs, higher pay and better schools and hospitals than rural areasNatural resources: fertile land, minerals or oil can raise income, if the revenue is used well
Ownership of wealth: people who own land, property, shares or firms receive rent, dividends and profit as well as wagesSector structure: economies based on low-value primary products tend to earn less than those based on manufacturing and services
Age and household size: pensioners and large families with one earner often have less income per personPopulation growth: if population grows faster than real GDP, real GDP per head falls
Discrimination: some groups may be paid less or find it harder to get good jobsStability and government: conflict, corruption and weak institutions discourage investment
Government policy: progressive taxes and state benefits narrow the gap; their absence leaves it wideGovernment policy: countries that tax and spend more on redistribution, and provide free schooling and healthcare, usually have a more even distribution of income
Using data (illustrative figures)
IndicatorCountry ACountry B
Real GDP per head$32,000$21,000
HDI0.780.84
Life expectancy at birth72 years79 years
Share of total income received by the richest 10% of households45%24%
Country A has the higher average income, but Country B has the higher HDI and life expectancy and a much more even distribution of income. A sensible conclusion is that the typical person in Country B probably enjoys the higher living standard, because Country A’s average is pulled up by a rich minority and its income is not being turned into health and education to the same extent.
Examiner Tip
When asked “Which country has higher living standards?” using data, never decide on one indicator alone. Compare real GDP per head and HDI (or life expectancy, years of schooling), then state the disadvantages of each measure. A balanced conclusion (“it depends on…”) earns the top marks on “Discuss” questions.

5.2 Poverty

Absolute and relative poverty

  • Absolute poverty: a situation where people do not have enough income to meet their basic needs — food, clean water, shelter, clothing and basic healthcare. It is often measured using an international poverty line (an income per day, in purchasing-power terms).
  • Relative poverty: a situation where people are poor compared with others in the same society, often defined as having an income below a certain percentage (e.g. 50% or 60%) of the median income. They can meet basic needs but cannot afford the standard of living most people enjoy.
Absolute povertyRelative poverty
Measured againstA fixed standard: the cost of basic needsOther people’s incomes in the same country
Where it is foundMostly in low-income countries, though some exists everywhereIn every country, rich or poor
If everyone’s income doublesFalls, because more people can afford basic needsUnchanged, because the gaps between people stay the same
Common Mistake
Saying relative poverty only exists in poor countries. Relative poverty exists in every country, including the richest, because it is measured against typical incomes in that country. Absolute poverty can be eliminated in theory; relative poverty is much harder to remove entirely while incomes are unequal.

Causes of poverty

The syllabus names five causes. Learn these first.

  • Unemployment — no earned income; the household may depend on low state benefits, or on nothing at all where there is no benefit system. The longer someone is out of work, the more their skills fade and the harder it is to get back in.
  • Low wages — people in low-skilled, low-productivity jobs may work full time and still not earn enough (“the working poor”). Workers in the informal sector have no minimum wage or legal protection.
  • Illness — poor health or disability limits the ability to work and earn, and medical bills use up income and savings where healthcare is not free. A carer in the family may also have to give up work.
  • Age — the elderly have stopped earning and may have little or no pension or savings; children depend on their parents’ income, so large families with one low earner are at risk; young workers have little experience and often the lowest pay.
  • Environmental factors — droughts, floods, storms and earthquakes destroy crops, homes and capital; poor soil, lack of clean water and a changing climate keep farm output low; pollution damages health. Poor households are hit hardest because they often live in the most exposed places and have no insurance or savings to recover.

Other causes worth knowing: lack of education and training (limits access to better-paid jobs), poor infrastructure and lack of access to finance, conflict, inflation reducing the real value of low fixed incomes, and a very unequal distribution of wealth and land.

Policies to alleviate poverty and redistribute income

The syllabus names six policies. For each one, be ready to explain how it works and one reason it may not succeed.

PolicyHow it helpsPossible drawback
Promoting economic growth (e.g. lower interest rates, infrastructure spending)Firms produce more, so they create jobs and incomes rise; higher tax revenue can fund help for the poorBenefits may not reach the poorest; may raise inflation or pollution
Improved educationRaises skills, productivity and earning power in the long runExpensive; takes many years to have an effect
Improved healthcare provisionHealthier people can work, are more productive and miss fewer days; free or cheap treatment stops medical bills pushing families into povertyHigh opportunity cost for the government budget; shortage of doctors and nurses
More generous state benefits (e.g. unemployment and child benefits, state pensions)Directly raises the income of the poorest; redistributes incomeCost to taxpayers; may reduce the incentive to seek work if benefits are close to low wages
Progressive taxationTakes a higher proportion of income from high earners, narrowing the gap in income after tax and funding benefits and public servicesMay reduce incentives to work and invest; tax avoidance
National minimum wage (NMW)Raises the pay of the lowest-paid workersMay cause unemployment if set above the equilibrium wage; does not help those without a job or in the informal sector

Alleviate or redistribute? Growth, education and healthcare mainly raise the incomes of the poor (alleviating absolute poverty). Progressive taxation and state benefits mainly redistribute income from richer to poorer households (reducing relative poverty). An NMW does some of both.

Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but useful extra examples for low-income countries: foreign aid and debt relief (funds schools, hospitals and infrastructure, with risks of corruption and dependency) and microfinance (small loans that help poor people start small businesses, though on a small scale and with a risk of debt problems).
1
CauseGovernment spends more on primary and secondary education.
2
EffectWorkers gain skills and become more productive.
3
EffectThey qualify for better-paid, higher-skilled jobs and are less likely to be unemployed.
4
OutcomeHousehold incomes rise above the poverty line; the next generation is also better educated, breaking the cycle of poverty.

5.3 Population

Factors that affect population growth: definitions

  • Birth rate: the number of live births per 1,000 of the population in a year.
  • Death rate: the number of deaths per 1,000 of the population in a year.
  • Immigration: people coming into a country to live there.
  • Emigration: people leaving a country to live elsewhere.
  • Net migration: the difference between immigration and emigration over a period (immigration − emigration). Positive = net immigration; negative = net emigration.
Birth rate
Live births per 1,000 people per year
Death rate
Deaths per 1,000 people per year
Natural increase
Birth rate − death rate
Net migration
Immigration − emigration
Population change
(Births − deaths) + net migration

Example: a birth rate of 22 per 1,000 and a death rate of 8 per 1,000 gives a natural increase of 14 per 1,000, i.e. 1.4% a year before migration.

Worked example (illustrative figures)
Country X has a population of 20 million, a birth rate of 30 per 1,000 and a death rate of 10 per 1,000. In the year, 150,000 people immigrate and 50,000 emigrate.
Births = 30 × 20,000 = 600,000. Deaths = 10 × 20,000 = 200,000. Natural increase = 400,000.
Net migration = 150,000 − 50,000 = +100,000.
Population change = 400,000 + 100,000 = +500,000, which is 500,000 ÷ 20,000,000 × 100 = 2.5% growth.

How birth rates, death rates and net migration vary between countries

Typical low-income countryTypical high-income country
Birth rateHighLow, sometimes below the death rate
Death rateHas fallen, but infant deaths are still relatively high; the overall rate can look low because the population is youngLow at each age, but the overall rate can be fairly high because a large share of people are elderly
Net migrationOften net emigrationOften net immigration
Population growthFastSlow, zero or negative

These are general patterns, not rules: always use the figures you are given.

Reasons why birth rates, death rates and net migration vary between countries

  • High birth rates in many low-income countries because:
    • children can work and support parents in old age (no state pensions);
    • high infant mortality encourages families to have more children;
    • limited access to, or knowledge of, contraception;
    • cultural and religious traditions; early marriage;
    • fewer women in education and paid work.
  • Low birth rates in high-income countries because children are expensive to raise and educate, more women pursue careers, people marry later, and contraception is widely available.
  • Death rates have fallen almost everywhere due to better healthcare, vaccinations, nutrition, clean water and sanitation. They remain higher where these are lacking or where there is conflict or disease, and in countries with a large share of elderly people.
  • Net migration: people move to countries with more jobs, higher wages, better public services or political stability (pull factors), and leave countries with conflict, persecution, poverty or climate-related disasters (push factors). Government immigration rules also matter.

The concept of an optimum population

  • The optimum population is the size of population that, combined with the country’s other resources and current technology, maximises output (real GDP) per head.
  • Under-population: too few people to make full use of resources — an increase in population would raise real GDP per head.
  • Over-population: too many people for the resources available — real GDP per head would be higher with a smaller population.
  • The optimum is not fixed: improvements in technology, capital and education raise it over time.

Effects of increases and decreases in population size

ChangePossible benefitsPossible problems
Increase in population sizeLarger labour force; bigger market for firms; economies of scale; more innovation; real GDP per head rises if the country was under-populatedPressure on housing, schools, healthcare, food and water; congestion; pollution; unemployment if jobs do not grow as fast; real GDP per head falls if the country is over-populated
Decrease in population sizeLess pressure on housing, land, public services and the environment; real GDP per head may rise if the country was over-populatedSmaller labour force and labour shortages; smaller home market, so firms may lose economies of scale; less tax revenue; usually comes with an ageing population
Net immigrationFills skill shortages; migrants are often of working age, so they pay taxes; widens the labour poolPressure on public services and housing; possible downward pressure on wages in some jobs
Net emigrationRemittances (money sent home) raise family incomes; may ease unemployment“Brain drain” — loss of skilled, young workers such as doctors and engineers

Effects of changes in the age distribution

ChangePossible benefitsPossible problems
Ageing population (a rising share of elderly people)Demand for new products (healthcare, leisure); older workers bring experience; voluntary workHigher spending on pensions and healthcare; smaller workforce; higher taxes on workers; labour shortages; less geographically and occupationally mobile labour
Young population (a large share of children)Large future workforce; potentially flexible, mobile labour laterHigh spending needed on education and child healthcare; many dependants now; jobs must be created quickly as they reach working age
Rising share of working-age peopleMore workers and taxpayers for each dependant; higher output and savingOnly a benefit if there are enough jobs; otherwise unemployment rises

Effects of changes in the gender distribution

Gender distribution is the balance between males and females in the population. It is usually close to equal, but it can shift.

  • More women than men at older ages: women live longer on average, so an ageing population has a rising share of elderly women, many living alone. This raises demand for pensions, healthcare and care services.
  • More men than women (for example, where many male workers immigrate for construction or mining jobs): the labour force is larger relative to the population, but fewer women of child-bearing age means a lower birth rate and slower population growth in future.
  • More women than men of working age (for example, where many men emigrate to find work): families may receive remittances, but the home country can face labour shortages in jobs traditionally done by men, and the birth rate may fall.
  • Any change in the balance alters the pattern of demand for goods and services, and the supply of labour to occupations where one gender is over-represented.

Population pyramids Background

The 2027–2029 syllabus no longer mentions population pyramids by name, but they are the usual way of showing age and gender distribution, so a data question may still use one. A population pyramid shows age groups on the vertical axis and the number or percentage of males (left) and females (right) on the horizontal axis.

ShapeTypical countryWhat it shows
Wide base, narrow top (triangle)Low-income, developingHigh birth rate, lower life expectancy, young population
Straighter sides, narrower base (column/beehive)High-income, developedLow birth rate, long life expectancy, ageing population
Base narrower than middle (inverted)Some high-income countriesVery low birth rate; population likely to shrink

Dependency ratio Background

  • The dependent population are those not of working age: young dependants (usually under 15/16) and elderly dependants (usually over 64/65).
  • Dependency ratio = (number of dependants ÷ number of people of working age) × 100.
  • A high ratio means each worker supports more dependants, putting pressure on taxes and government spending. It is a handy way to explain the cost of an ageing or very young population.
  • Example (illustrative): 8 million young and 4 million elderly dependants with 24 million people of working age gives (12 ÷ 24) × 100 = 50, i.e. 50 dependants for every 100 people of working age.
Model answer
Explain two reasons why an ageing population may reduce a country’s economic growth. (4 marks)
First, an ageing population means a smaller proportion of people are of working age. The labour force shrinks, so the country has fewer workers to produce goods and services, reducing its productive capacity and real GDP. Second, the government has to spend more on state pensions and healthcare for the elderly. This may require higher taxes on workers and firms, reducing incentives to work and invest, or it may mean less government spending on infrastructure and education, which lowers future growth.
Examiner Tip
For “Discuss whether a larger population always benefits an economy” (8 marks), give developed arguments on both sides (larger workforce and market vs pressure on resources and lower real GDP per head), then link to optimum population: the answer depends on whether the country is currently under- or over-populated, the age structure of the extra people, and whether investment and jobs keep pace.

5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

Countries are often grouped as low-income (less developed), middle-income and high-income (more developed). The syllabus lists eight differences. For each one you should be able to explain why it arises (cause) and what follows from it (consequence).

Difference inLow-income / less developedHigh-income / more developed
IncomeLow real GDP per head; more absolute poverty; often high inequalityHigh real GDP per head; little absolute poverty
ProductivityLow output per worker: little capital, basic technology, low skillsHigh output per worker: advanced capital and technology, skilled labour
Population growthHigh birth rate, rapid growth, young populationLow birth rate, slow or negative growth, ageing population
Size of primary, secondary and tertiary sectorsLarge primary sector (agriculture, mining); large informal sectorLarge tertiary sector (services); small primary sector; secondary sector shrinking relative to services
Saving and investmentLow incomes → low saving → low investment in capitalHigher saving and developed banks → more investment
EducationFewer years of schooling and lower literacy, often especially for girlsHigh literacy; widespread secondary and higher education
HealthcareLower life expectancy, higher infant mortality, limited clean water and doctorsHigh life expectancy, low infant mortality, widespread healthcare
Natural resourcesMay have few resources, or have plenty but depend on exporting one or two raw commodities at unstable pricesMay have plenty or few, but have the capital, skills and technology to process resources or to import them and add value

Causes and consequences of each difference

Difference inWhy it matters (cause of the development gap)Consequence
IncomeLow income leaves little for anything beyond necessitiesLow spending, low saving and low tax revenue, so the government cannot afford good schools, hospitals and infrastructure
ProductivityWorkers with little capital, training or technology produce less per hourLow wages and uncompetitive exports; high-productivity countries earn more and can attract investment
