Population growthRapid growth means output must grow just as fast to keep real GDP per head from fallingResources go into feeding, housing and schooling more children instead of investment; slow growth in rich countries brings ageing and labour shortages
Size of sectorsPrimary products usually have low value added and unstable prices; manufacturing and services add more valuePrimary-based economies have lower and less reliable incomes; countries develop as workers move into secondary and tertiary jobs
Saving and investmentWithout saving, banks have little to lend, so firms cannot buy capital goodsProductive capacity grows slowly; countries may rely on foreign investment, loans or aid
EducationEducation builds the skills of the labour forceA skilled labour force is more productive, adapts to new technology and attracts multinational companies (MNCs); low education keeps workers in low-paid jobs
HealthcareHealthy people can work, learn and live longerPoor health means lost working days, lower productivity and income spent on treatment; good healthcare raises life expectancy and HDI
Natural resourcesFertile land, minerals, oil, a coastline or a good climate give a country something to produce and exportExport revenue can fund development, but only if it is invested widely; resources can run out, prices can fall, and extraction can damage the environment. Some countries with few resources have developed through education, trade and investment instead

Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors

  • Primary sector: extraction of natural resources (farming, fishing, forestry, mining).
  • Secondary sector: manufacturing and construction — turning raw materials into goods.
  • Tertiary sector: providing services (banking, retail, tourism, education, healthcare).
  • As countries develop, employment and output usually shift from primary → secondary → tertiary.

The cycle of poverty (how low saving and investment keep development low)

1
Low incomesMost income is spent on necessities, leaving little to save.
2
Low savingBanks have few funds to lend to firms.
3
Low investmentLittle new capital, technology, education or infrastructure.
4
Low productivityLow output per worker keeps wages and incomes low — and the cycle repeats.

Breaking the cycle may require investment by multinational companies (MNCs), aid, debt relief, better access to international markets (fewer trade restrictions by rich countries), investment in education and healthcare, and reducing corruption.

Common Mistake
Treating economic growth and economic development as the same thing. Growth is an increase in real GDP; development is an improvement in overall welfare. A country can grow (e.g. by exporting oil) while most people see little improvement in health, education or poverty, and while environmental damage harms future living standards.
Real GDP per head
Real GDP ÷ population
HDI components
Health, education, income (0 to 1)
Absolute poverty
Cannot afford basic needs
Relative poverty
Poor compared with others in the country
Net migration
Immigration − emigration
Optimum population
Real GDP per head at its highest

Quick Checklist

  • 5.1 I can define real GDP per head and HDI, name the three HDI components, and give advantages and disadvantages of each indicator.
  • 5.1 I can explain why living standards and income distribution differ within a country and between countries, and compare two countries using data.
  • 5.2 I can explain the difference between absolute and relative poverty.
  • 5.2 I can explain the five causes of poverty: unemployment, low wages, illness, age and environmental factors.
  • 5.2 I can explain and evaluate the six policies: promoting economic growth, improved education, improved healthcare provision, more generous state benefits, progressive taxation and a national minimum wage.
  • 5.3 I can define birth rate, death rate, immigration, emigration and net migration, and calculate a change in population.
  • 5.3 I can describe how, and explain why, birth rates, death rates and net migration vary between countries.
  • 5.3 I can explain optimum population, under-population and over-population.
  • 5.3 I can analyse the effects of an increase or decrease in population size and of changes in the age and gender distribution.
  • 5.4 I can explain the causes and consequences of differences between countries in income, productivity, population growth, sector sizes, saving and investment, education, healthcare and natural resources.
Topic 6 · International Trade

International Trade and Globalisation

Four sub-topics: 6.1 specialisation and free trade, 6.2 globalisation and trade restrictions (including multinational companies), 6.3 foreign exchange rates, and 6.4 the current account of the balance of payments. This topic is a favourite for data-response questions using trade and exchange rate figures.

6.1 Specialisation and free trade

Specialisation by country

Specialisation by country occurs when a country concentrates on producing a limited range of goods and services, and trades to obtain the others.

The basis for specialisation. A country should specialise in the products where its resources are allocated best and/or where it can produce at low cost compared with other countries. This depends on the factors of production it has: climate and land, natural resources, the size and skills of its labour force, capital and technology. Resources then go to the use where they give up the least other output (the lowest opportunity cost).

  • Examples: Saudi Arabia (oil), Bangladesh (garments), Switzerland (financial services, pharmaceuticals), New Zealand (dairy).
  • Illustration: Country X has fertile land and a warm climate, so it can grow rice more cheaply than Country Y. Country Y has skilled engineers and modern factories, so it can make machinery more cheaply. If each specialises and they trade, total output of both goods can be higher than if each tried to make everything.
Advantages of specialisation by countryDisadvantages of specialisation by country
Higher total world output; more efficient use of resources; economies of scale lower average costs and prices; export earnings; wider choice for consumers through trade; workers and firms build up skills and reputationOver-dependence on a few products; vulnerable to falls in world demand or price; risk of structural unemployment if demand shifts; depletion of natural resources; reliance on imports for essentials (a risk if supplies are cut off); more transport emissions
Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but specialisation also happens at regional level within a country (a region known for car manufacturing, wine or technology firms). The region gains a skilled labour pool and nearby suppliers, but suffers regional unemployment if its industry declines.

Free trade

Free trade is international trade without government restrictions (no tariffs, quotas or other barriers). It allows countries to specialise fully.

Advantages of free tradeDisadvantages of free trade
Lower prices for consumers as the most efficient producers supply the marketDomestic firms that cannot compete with imports may close, causing structural unemployment
Greater choice and variety of productsNew (infant) industries may never get the chance to grow against established foreign rivals
Larger markets for domestic firms, allowing economies of scaleRisk of dumping by foreign firms
Increased competition encourages efficiency, innovation and qualityOver-dependence on other countries for essentials such as food or energy
Access to raw materials and capital goods not available at homeDemerit goods can be imported more easily; more transport and production may harm the environment
Higher world output and living standards through specialisationThe government collects no tariff revenue

6.2 Globalisation and trade restrictions

Definition of globalisation

Globalisation is the process by which the world’s economies become increasingly integrated and interdependent through trade in goods and services, flows of capital, movement of labour, and the spread of technology and ideas.

Causes of changes in globalisation

Globalisation can speed up, slow down or even go into reverse. The syllabus names four causes:

CauseGlobalisation increases when…Globalisation slows or reverses when…
Changes in trade restrictionsTariffs and quotas are reduced or removed (e.g. through trade agreements), so trade is cheaper and easierCountries raise tariffs or impose new quotas and embargoes (a trade war)
Changes in transport costsContainer ships, larger aircraft and better ports make it cheaper to move goods long distancesFuel prices rise or shipping routes are disrupted, so buying from far away costs more
Changes in communication costsCheaper internet and phone services let firms manage factories, sell and provide services across bordersCommunication becomes dearer or is restricted between countries
Movement of multinational companies (MNCs)MNCs set up production in more countries, bringing investment and linking economies togetherMNCs close overseas plants and move production back to the home country

Effects of changes in globalisation

The table shows the effects of an increase in globalisation. A fall in globalisation tends to have the opposite effects.

Effect on…What may happenBut…
International tradeExports and imports grow; countries specialise more and become more interdependentA problem in one country (a recession, a factory shutdown) spreads quickly to its trading partners
CompetitionFirms face more foreign rivals, which pushes prices down and quality and efficiency upLess efficient domestic firms may close; large MNCs may come to dominate some markets
The environmentMore production and more transport raise emissions and use up resources; firms may move to countries with weaker environmental rulesCleaner technology spreads between countries, and higher incomes give governments more funds to protect the environment
MigrationIt is easier for workers to move to countries with higher wages; this fills skill shortages there and migrants send remittances homeCountries losing skilled workers suffer a “brain drain”; receiving countries may face pressure on housing and public services
Income distributionThe gap between countries may narrow as lower-income countries gain jobs and investmentThe gap within a country may widen: skilled workers and owners of firms gain most, while low-skilled workers in industries competing with imports may lose jobs or see lower pay
Economic developmentJobs, higher incomes, new technology and more tax revenue for education and healthcare can reduce poverty and raise living standardsThe benefits are uneven; a country may become dependent on a few MNCs or export markets

Role of multinational companies (MNCs)

A multinational company (MNC) is a firm that produces goods or services in more than one country. The home country is where its headquarters are; a host country is another country where it has operations.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Host countryCreates jobs and raises incomes; investment in capital and infrastructure; transfer of technology and skills; tax revenue; exports improve the current account; more choice for consumersProfits sent back to the home country; local firms may be forced out; jobs may be low-skilled and low-paid; possible exploitation of workers; environmental damage and resource depletion; MNC may leave suddenly; political influence
Home countryProfits flow back, raising national income; MNC grows, gaining economies of scale; cheaper production abroad can lower prices for home consumersJobs lost when production moves abroad; lower tax revenue if profits are declared elsewhere; less investment at home

Types of trade restrictions (methods of protection)

Trade restrictions (also called methods of protection, or protectionism in older papers) are government measures that limit free trade, usually to protect domestic industries from foreign competition. The syllabus names four:

MethodDefinitionEffect
TariffA tax on imported goodsRaises the price of imports, reduces the quantity imported, raises government revenue
Import quotaA limit on the quantity (or value) of a good that can be importedReduces the supply of imports, so their price rises; no tax revenue unless import licences are sold
SubsidyA government payment to domestic producers that lowers their costsDomestic goods become cheaper and more competitive against imports and in export markets; costs the government money
EmbargoA complete ban on trade (imports and/or exports) with a country or in a productTrade in that product or with that country stops; often used for political, safety or security reasons
Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but governments also restrict imports in less obvious ways, such as strict product standards and extra paperwork at the border.

Reasons for trade restrictions

  • Protect infant (sunrise) industries: new industries need time to grow and gain economies of scale before they can compete with established foreign rivals.
  • Protect declining (sunset) industries: slowing the decline avoids sudden structural unemployment and gives workers time to retrain and move to other jobs.
  • Protect strategic industries: food, energy and defence, so the country does not depend on others for essentials.
  • Avoid dumping: dumping is when foreign firms sell in another country at a price below their cost of production, to drive out domestic competitors.
  • Reduce a deficit on the current account of the balance of payments: restrictions cut spending on imports.
  • Raise tax revenue: tariffs bring in revenue for the government.
  • Restrict the import of demerit goods: e.g. high tariffs or bans on imported cigarettes, alcohol or unsafe products, to protect consumers’ health.
  • Promote environmental sustainability: e.g. tariffs on goods made with high carbon emissions, bans on imports of illegally logged timber or products from endangered species; this protects the environment and stops firms in countries with strict rules being undercut by polluters.

Consequences of trade restrictions

Impact on…AdvantagesDisadvantages
The home country (the one imposing the restriction)Output and jobs in protected industries are saved or grow; infant industries get a chance to develop; tariff revenue; fewer imports can improve the current account; fewer demerit or polluting goods come inHigher prices and less choice for consumers; higher costs for firms that use imported raw materials and components; protected firms face less competition, so may become inefficient and less innovative; subsidies have an opportunity cost; exporters suffer if other countries retaliate
Trading partnersFew. Firms there may be pushed to find new markets or become more efficientTheir exports fall, so output, employment and incomes in export industries fall; their current account may worsen; they may retaliate with restrictions of their own (a trade war)

Overall, restricting free trade means countries specialise less, so world output and living standards tend to be lower. Protection is easier to justify when it is temporary and has a clear purpose (an infant industry, dumping) than when it shelters inefficient firms for years.

Chain of reasoning: a tariff on imported steel

1
CauseGovernment places a tariff on imported steel.
2
EffectThe price of imported steel rises, so domestic buyers switch to domestically produced steel.
3
EffectDomestic steel output and employment increase; government gains tariff revenue.
4
OutcomeBut car makers and builders pay more for steel, raising their costs and prices, and the exporting country (the trading partner) loses sales and may retaliate against this country’s exports.
Common Mistake
Confusing a tariff with a quota. A tariff is a tax (it raises price and earns government revenue); a quota is a quantity limit. Also, a subsidy protects by lowering domestic firms’ costs — it does not directly make imports more expensive.

6.3 Foreign exchange rates

Definition of foreign exchange rate

The foreign exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another (e.g. RM1 = US$0.25). The foreign exchange market is where currencies are bought and sold.

Reasons for buying and selling foreign currencies

Anyone who buys a currency adds to the demand for it; anyone who sells it adds to its supply. The examples use the Malaysian ringgit (RM).

ReasonCreates demand for ringgit (buying)Creates supply of ringgit (selling)
Trade in goods and servicesForeigners buy Malaysian exports; foreign tourists visit MalaysiaMalaysians buy imports or travel abroad, so sell ringgit for foreign currency
SpeculationSpeculators expect the ringgit to rise, so buy now to sell later at a profitSpeculators expect the ringgit to fall, so sell now
Government intervention in currency marketsThe central bank buys ringgit with its reserves of foreign currency to push the price upThe central bank sells ringgit for foreign currency to push the price down
Payment of profit, interest and dividends between countriesMalaysian firms and savers bring home profit, interest and dividends earned abroadForeign MNCs in Malaysia send profit home; interest and dividends are paid to foreign lenders and shareholders
Workers’ remittancesMalaysians working abroad send part of their pay home to their familiesForeign workers in Malaysia send part of their pay to their home countries
Investment in capital goods between countriesA foreign firm builds a factory in Malaysia and needs ringgit to pay for itA Malaysian firm builds a factory abroad and needs foreign currency

Determination of the foreign exchange rate in the foreign exchange market

Floating exchange rate
Set by market forces: the demand for and supply of the currency
Appreciation
A rise in the value of a currency caused by market forces
Depreciation
A fall in the value of a currency caused by market forces
Equilibrium rate
Where demand for the currency equals supply
  • The demand curve for a currency slopes down: when the ringgit is cheaper, Malaysian exports cost foreigners less, so they buy more of them and need more ringgit.
  • The supply curve slopes up: when the ringgit is worth more, imports cost Malaysians less, so they buy more of them and sell more ringgit.
  • The equilibrium foreign exchange rate is where the demand for the currency equals its supply. A change in any of the reasons above shifts demand or supply and moves the rate.

Causes of foreign exchange rate fluctuations

  • Changes in demand for exports and imports: higher export sales raise demand for the currency (appreciation); higher spending on imports raises its supply (depreciation). For example, if a country’s inflation is higher than its trading partners’, its exports become less competitive and imports more attractive, so the currency depreciates.
  • Changes in the interest rate: a higher interest rate attracts savings from abroad (“hot money”), raising demand for the currency, so it appreciates. A lower interest rate does the opposite.
  • Speculation: if speculators expect a currency to rise they buy it, which raises demand and makes it rise; if they expect a fall they sell it, which raises supply and makes it fall.

The other reasons for buying and selling currencies shift the curves in the same way: for example, MNCs investing in a country raise demand for its currency, and a central bank selling its own currency raises supply.

Consequences of changes in foreign exchange rates

Effect on…AppreciationDepreciation
Export prices (in foreign currency)Rise → exports less competitiveFall → exports more competitive
Demand for exportsFallsRises
Import prices (in domestic currency)Fall → imports cheaperRise → imports dearer
Demand for importsRisesFalls
Current accountTends to worsen (if demand is price elastic)Tends to improve (if demand is price elastic)
InflationLower: cheaper imported goods and raw materials; firms under pressure to keep costs downHigher: dearer imported goods and raw materials (cost-push)
Employment and growthMay fall in export industries and industries competing with importsMay rise as export demand and total demand increase
Worked example: a depreciation
The ringgit depreciates from RM1 = US$0.25 to RM1 = US$0.20 (illustrative figures).
Export price: a Malaysian-made shirt costs RM200. Its price in the USA falls from 200 × 0.25 = US$50 to 200 × 0.20 = US$40, so Americans demand more Malaysian shirts.
Import price: an American phone costs US$100. Its price in Malaysia rises from 100 ÷ 0.25 = RM400 to 100 ÷ 0.20 = RM500, so Malaysians demand fewer American phones.
The ringgit price of the shirt and the dollar price of the phone have not changed. Only the price in the other currency has. An appreciation works the other way round.
Strong Pound Imports Cheaper Exports Dearer — SPICED
Examiner Tip
Always say whose price changes and in which currency. “A depreciation of the rupee makes Indian exports cheaper in foreign currency and imports dearer in rupees.” Then add a condition: the current account only improves if demand for exports and imports is price elastic.

Fixed exchange rates Background

Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus, but you will meet these terms in older past papers. A fixed exchange rate is set by the government or central bank against another currency and kept there by buying or selling the currency with reserves, or by changing interest rates. It gives certainty to traders and investors but needs large reserves to defend. When a government raises a fixed rate it is a revaluation; when it lowers it, a devaluation. (Appreciation and depreciation are the words for a floating rate.)

6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

Structure of the current account

The balance of payments is a record of all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world over a period of time, usually a year. The current account records trade in goods and services plus income flows and transfers. It has four components:

ComponentWhat it recordsExample of a credit (money in)Example of a debit (money out)
Trade in goodsExports and imports of physical goods (visible trade)Selling cars abroadBuying oil from abroad
Trade in servicesExports and imports of services (invisible trade)Foreign tourists visiting; insurance sold abroadResidents taking holidays abroad
Primary incomeIncome earned from factors of production used abroad: profit, interest, dividends and wagesProfit from a firm’s overseas branch sent homeA foreign MNC sending its profit to its home country
Secondary incomeTransfers with nothing given in returnRemittances from citizens working abroad; foreign aid receivedForeign workers sending remittances home; aid given
Balance of each component
Credits (money in) − debits (money out)
Current account balance
Goods balance + services balance + primary income balance + secondary income balance
Deficit
Debits (outflows) exceed credits (inflows): a negative balance
Surplus
Credits (inflows) exceed debits (outflows): a positive balance
Worked calculation
Country X’s current account for one year (illustrative figures, US$ billion):
ComponentCreditsDebitsBalance
Trade in goods120160120 − 160 = −40 (deficit)
Trade in services654065 − 40 = +25 (surplus)
Primary income201520 − 15 = +5 (surplus)
Secondary income4124 − 12 = −8 (deficit)
Current account209227−18 (deficit)
Current account balance = −40 + 25 + 5 − 8 = −US$18bn (a deficit). Check: total credits 209 − total debits 227 = −18.
Balance of trade in goods and services = −40 + 25 = −US$15bn.

Causes of current account deficit and surplus

Reasons for a deficit:

  • High domestic incomes / consumer boom — more spending on imports.
  • Lack of international competitiveness — high inflation, low productivity, high costs or poor quality.
  • A high (appreciated) exchange rate — exports dearer, imports cheaper.
  • Recession abroad — lower demand for the country’s exports.
  • Lack of natural resources, so raw materials and fuel must be imported; outflows of profits to foreign MNCs.

Reasons for a surplus: the reverse. Strong competitiveness (low inflation, high productivity, good quality), a low exchange rate, high world demand for its exports (e.g. commodities at high prices), low domestic demand for imports, or large inflows of profit and remittances from abroad.

Consequences of current account deficit and surplus

Impact on…DeficitSurplus
GDPMore money leaves the country than enters, so total demand (aggregate demand) is lower; GDP may fall or grow more slowlyNet inflow of money raises total demand; GDP tends to rise
EmploymentFewer jobs in export industries and in industries competing with importsMore jobs in export industries
InflationLower total demand reduces demand-pull pressure; but if the currency depreciates, dearer imports can raise pricesHigher total demand may cause demand-pull inflation; but if the currency appreciates, cheaper imports hold prices down
Foreign exchange rateMore of the currency is sold (to pay for imports) than bought, so a floating rate tends to depreciateMore of the currency is bought than sold, so a floating rate tends to appreciate
  • A deficit must also be financed by borrowing from abroad, selling assets or running down reserves. It is less of a concern if it is small or short-term, or if the imports are capital goods that raise future productivity.
  • A surplus is not all good news: residents consume fewer goods and services than the country could afford, and trading partners with deficits may respond with trade restrictions.

Policies to achieve balance of payments stability

Balance of payments stability means avoiding a large, lasting deficit or surplus on the current account. Most exam questions ask about reducing a deficit:

PolicyHow it reduces a deficitHow effective?
Contractionary fiscal policy (higher taxes, lower government spending)Reduces incomes and so spending on importsWorks fairly quickly, but lowers growth and raises unemployment; does not fix poor competitiveness
Contractionary monetary policy (higher interest rates)Reduces borrowing and spending on imports; lowers inflation, improving competitivenessMay attract savings from abroad so the currency appreciates, making exports dearer; slows growth
Allowing or encouraging the currency to depreciateMakes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at homeOnly works if demand for exports and imports is price elastic; dearer imports add to inflation
Trade restrictions (tariffs, import quotas, subsidies)Reduce imports directly, or help domestic firms competeRisk of retaliation; higher prices; protected firms may stay inefficient; may break trade agreements
Supply-side policies (education, training, infrastructure, investment incentives)Raise productivity and quality, improving long-run competitivenessTackles the root cause, but expensive and slow to take effect

To reduce a large surplus, the policies run the other way: expansionary fiscal or monetary policy to raise spending on imports, removing trade restrictions, or letting the currency appreciate.

Model answer
Explain how a rise in a country’s inflation rate could cause a current account deficit. (4 marks)
If the country’s inflation rate rises above that of its trading partners, its goods and services become relatively more expensive. Foreign buyers switch to cheaper products from other countries, so the value of the country’s exports falls. At the same time, domestic consumers find imports relatively cheaper than domestically produced goods, so spending on imports rises. With export revenue falling and import spending rising, debits exceed credits, causing a deficit on the trade in goods and services and so on the current account.

Quick Checklist

  • 6.1 I can define specialisation by country, explain its basis (best resource allocation, low-cost production) and give its advantages and disadvantages.
  • 6.1 I can define free trade and explain its advantages and disadvantages.
  • 6.2 I can define globalisation, give the four causes of changes in it and explain its effects on trade, competition, the environment, migration, income distribution and economic development.
  • 6.2 I can analyse the advantages and disadvantages of MNCs for host and home countries.
  • 6.2 I can define tariffs, import quotas, subsidies and embargoes, give the eight reasons for trade restrictions and explain the consequences for the home country and its trading partners.
  • 6.3 I can define the foreign exchange rate and give the six reasons for buying and selling currencies.
  • 6.3 I can define floating exchange rate, appreciation and depreciation, and draw a foreign exchange market diagram showing each.
  • 6.3 I can explain the three causes of exchange rate fluctuations and work out how a change in the rate affects export and import prices and demand.
  • 6.4 I can name the four components of the current account and calculate the balance of each and of the whole account.
  • 6.4 I can explain the causes of a current account deficit and surplus, their impact on GDP, employment, inflation and the foreign exchange rate, and how effective the policies to achieve balance of payments stability are.
Illustrated Examples

Illustrated Examples: See the Economics

Twelve original worked examples, two for each syllabus topic, each built around a diagram drawn to scale: production possibility curves, demand and supply, elasticity and revenue, the labour market, costs, the government budget, unemployment and inflation, living standards, population, foreign exchange rates and the current account. Read the values off the picture, cover the answer and work it out yourself, then compare.

Example 1: Reading opportunity cost off a PPC

Practice question · Topic 1.4 · [6 marks]

Country X uses all its resources to produce two goods, wheat and machines. The diagram shows its production possibility curve (PPC), drawn to scale. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of increasing the output of machines from 10 thousand to 20 thousand. [2] (b) Describe how the opportunity cost of machines changes as more machines are produced. Use figures from the diagram. [2] (c) Explain what point U shows about Country X’s economy. [2]

(a) This is a movement along the PPC from A to B. Wheat output falls from 80 million tonnes to 50 million tonnes (1). The opportunity cost of the extra 10 thousand machines is 80 − 50 = 30 million tonnes of wheat (1).

(b) The opportunity cost rises as more machines are made (1). The first 10 thousand machines cost 10 million tonnes of wheat (90 to 80), the next 10 thousand cost 30 million tonnes (80 to 50) and the last 10 thousand cost 50 million tonnes (50 to 0) (1).

(c) Point U is under (inside) the PPC: Country X is producing 10 thousand machines and 50 million tonnes of wheat, which is less than it is able to produce (1). Some resources are unemployed or being used inefficiently, for example workers without jobs or farmland left idle (1). Moving from U up to A would give 30 million tonnes more wheat with no machines given up, so there is no opportunity cost.

Why this scores
Opportunity cost is always stated in units of the other good: the answer to (a) is “30 million tonnes of wheat”, not “10 thousand machines” and not a sum of money. In (b) the figures prove the pattern. The PPC bows outwards because resources are not equally good at making both goods, so each extra batch of machines takes resources that were better suited to wheat.

Example 2: A PPC shift and economic growth

Practice question · Topic 1.4 · [6 marks]

Country Y produces agricultural goods and manufactured goods. After several years of investment in new factories, irrigation and worker training, its production possibility curve shifts from PPC to PPC1 and the economy moves from point A to point B. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the maximum possible output of manufactured goods. [2] (b) Explain why the shift from PPC to PPC1 shows economic growth. [2] (c) Explain, using the figures at A and B, why the move from A to B was not possible before the shift. [2]

(a) Maximum output of manufactured goods rises from 60 million units to 90 million units, an increase of 30 million (1). Percentage increase = 30 ÷ 60 × 100 = 50% (1).

(b) An outward shift means the economy’s productive capacity has increased: with all resources fully used, Country Y can now make more of both goods than before (1). This happened because the quantity and quality of its factors of production rose: more capital goods (factories, irrigation) and more skilled labour (1).

(c) At A, Country Y produces 15 million tonnes of agricultural goods and 45 million units of manufactured goods. At B it produces 30 million tonnes and 50 million units, so output of both goods is higher (1). B lies beyond the original PPC, so it was unattainable with the old resources: on PPC, producing 30 million tonnes of agricultural goods would have left no resources for manufactured goods at all (1).

Examiner Tip
Keep two ideas apart. A movement along a PPC reallocates the same resources, so more of one good means less of the other. A shift of the PPC changes what is possible. In this example agricultural capacity also grows by 50% (30 to 45 million tonnes), so the whole curve moves out. Growth is not free, though: the resources used to build the factories could have made consumer goods at the time.

Example 3: From a schedule to equilibrium and a shortage

Practice question · Topics 2.4 and 2.10 · [6 marks]

The table shows the monthly demand and supply schedule for rice in Country Z. The diagram plots the same figures. (a) Identify the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity. [2] (b) The government sets a maximum price of $3 per kg. Calculate the shortage of rice this causes. [2] (c) Explain why the maximum price causes a shortage. [2]

Price ($ per kg)Quantity demanded (million kg)Quantity supplied (million kg)
11200
210020
38040
46060
54080
620100

(a) Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. In the schedule this is the row where both are 60, and on the diagram it is point E where D and S cross: equilibrium price $4 per kg (1), equilibrium quantity 60 million kg (1).

(b) At $3, quantity demanded is 80 million kg and quantity supplied is 40 million kg (1). Shortage = 80 − 40 = 40 million kg per month (1).

(c) The maximum price is below the equilibrium price. The lower price causes an extension in demand, from 60 to 80 million kg, because rice is now more affordable (1). It also causes a contraction in supply, from 60 to 40 million kg, because growing rice is less profitable; the price is not allowed to rise to remove the gap, so demand stays greater than supply (1).

Why this scores
A shortage is measured along the quantity axis at the controlled price: read across the $3 line to S (40) and to D (80). It is not the $1 gap between the two prices. Notice too that only 40 million kg are actually sold, which is less than the 60 million kg traded at equilibrium. A maximum price set above $4 would have no effect at all.

Example 4: PED and the two revenue rectangles

Practice question · Topic 2.6 · [6 marks]

Aurora Cinema cuts its ticket price from $10 to $8. Weekly ticket sales rise from 400 to 600, as shown by points A and B on the diagram. (a) Calculate the price elasticity of demand (PED) for tickets. Show your working. [2] (b) Calculate the change in the cinema’s weekly revenue. [2] (c) Explain, using the diagram, why revenue changed in this way. [2]

(a) % change in quantity demanded = 200 ÷ 400 × 100 = +50%. % change in price = −2 ÷ 10 × 100 = −20% (1). PED = 50 ÷ −20 = −2.5 (1). The figure is greater than 1 (ignoring the sign), so demand is price elastic.

(b) Revenue before = $10 × 400 = $4 000. Revenue after = $8 × 600 = $4 800 (1). Revenue rises by $800 a week (1).

(c) Demand is price elastic, so the 20% price cut brings a larger (50%) rise in quantity demanded (1). On the diagram the revenue gained from 200 extra tickets at $8 ($1 600) is bigger than the revenue lost by charging $2 less on the first 400 tickets ($800), so total revenue rises by $1 600 − $800 = $800 (1).

Examiner Tip
Always divide by the original figure (400 tickets, $10) when working out a percentage change, and put quantity on top in the PED formula. A quick check: when demand is elastic, price and revenue move in opposite directions; when demand is inelastic they move in the same direction. If the “lost” strip on your diagram were bigger than the “gained” block, the price cut would have reduced revenue.

Example 5: A national minimum wage on a labour-market diagram

Practice question · Topic 3.3 · [8 marks]

The diagram shows the market for fruit pickers in Country W. (a) Identify the equilibrium wage rate and the number of workers employed at equilibrium. [2] (b) The government introduces a national minimum wage (NMW) of $7 per hour. Calculate the excess supply of labour this causes. [2] (c) Analyse how the NMW affects workers in this market. [4]

(a) Demand for labour and supply of labour cross at E: the equilibrium wage rate is $6 per hour (1) and 60 thousand workers are employed (1).

(b) At $7 per hour, firms demand 50 thousand workers and 80 thousand workers are willing to work (1). Excess supply of labour = 80 − 50 = 30 thousand workers (1).

(c) The 50 thousand workers who keep their jobs gain: their wage rises from $6 to $7 per hour, about 17% more, so they can afford more goods and services (1). However, labour is now more expensive, so firms’ demand for labour contracts from 60 thousand to 50 thousand and 10 thousand pickers lose their jobs and their wage income (1). The higher wage also attracts more people into this market: supply of labour extends from 60 thousand to 80 thousand, so another 20 thousand people look for picking work but cannot find it (1). Altogether 30 thousand people who want to work at $7 are unemployed, so the NMW helps those in work at the expense of those who are not (1).

Why this scores
The answer reads three numbers off the NMW line (50, 60 and 80) and explains each gap, instead of just writing “unemployment rises”. The excess supply of 30 thousand has two parts: 10 thousand jobs lost (60 to 50) plus 20 thousand new job-seekers (60 to 80). An NMW only has these effects when it is set above the equilibrium wage. For a “Discuss” question you would add the other side: the size of the job loss depends on how much firms’ demand for labour responds to the wage, and better-paid workers may be more motivated and productive.

Example 6: A cost table and the ATC curve

Practice question · Topics 3.4 and 3.6 · [8 marks]

Nkosi Chairs is a small firm making wooden chairs. Its fixed cost is $6 000 per week. The table shows its variable cost at different levels of output. (a) Calculate the total cost (TC), average total cost (ATC), average fixed cost (AFC) and average variable cost (AVC) when output is 200 chairs per week. [4] (b) Identify, from the diagram, the output at which ATC is lowest and the ATC at that output. [2] (c) Explain why ATC rises when output increases beyond 300 chairs per week. [2]

Output (chairs per week)Fixed cost, FC ($)Variable cost, VC ($)
1006 0005 000
2006 0008 000
3006 00012 000
4006 00020 000
5006 00034 000

(a) At 200 chairs:

  • TC = FC + VC = 6 000 + 8 000 = $14 000 (1)
  • ATC = TC ÷ output = 14 000 ÷ 200 = $70 per chair (1)
  • AFC = FC ÷ output = 6 000 ÷ 200 = $30 per chair (1)
  • AVC = VC ÷ output = 8 000 ÷ 200 = $40 per chair (1)

Check: AFC + AVC = 30 + 40 = 70 = ATC. Doing the same for every row gives the full table, and the ATC column is what the diagram plots.

Output (chairs per week)TC ($)ATC ($ per chair)AFC ($ per chair)AVC ($ per chair)
10011 0001106050
20014 000703040
30018 000602040
40026 000651550
50040 000801268

(b) ATC is lowest at an output of 300 chairs per week (1), where it is $60 per chair (1).

(c) Beyond 300 chairs the firm experiences diseconomies of scale: for example, a larger workforce is harder to manage and communication is slower, or workers must be paid higher overtime rates, so variable cost per chair rises (1). In the table AVC climbs from $40 to $68 between 300 and 500 chairs, which is more than the fall in AFC from $20 to $12, so ATC rises from $60 to $80 (1).

Why this scores
Every calculation starts with the formula, then the figures, then an answer with units ($ per chair for the three averages). Two patterns are worth remembering. AFC always falls as output rises, because the same $6 000 is spread over more chairs. ATC is U-shaped: it falls while the firm gains economies of scale (such as bulk-buying wood more cheaply) and rises once diseconomies of scale outweigh them. On an ATC diagram, label the lowest point and mark the two sides, as here.

Example 7: Reading a government budget from a bar chart

Practice question · Topic 4.2 · [4 marks]

The diagram shows the government revenue and government spending of Tavora for three years. (a) Calculate Tavora’s government budget balance in each year, stating whether it is a deficit or a surplus. [3] (b) Identify the year in which the government had to borrow the most. [1]

Answer (budget balance = government revenue − government spending):

YearRevenue ($bn)Spending ($bn)WorkingBudget balance
2024180204180 − 204 = −24Deficit of $24 billion (1)
2025196208196 − 208 = −12Deficit of $12 billion (1)
2026215209215 − 209 = +6Surplus of $6 billion (1)

(b) 2024 (1). It has the largest deficit, and a deficit has to be covered by borrowing.

You can see the answer before you calculate it: in 2024 and 2025 the spending bar is taller than the revenue bar (deficit), and in 2026 the revenue bar is taller (surplus).

Why this scores
Each answer has a size, a unit and a label: “deficit of $24 billion”, not just “−24”. Notice also that spending rose every year, yet the deficit shrank, because revenue rose faster. Do not assume that a smaller deficit means the government cut its spending.

Example 8: Inflation from a CPI line graph

Practice question · Topic 4.7 · [6 marks]

The diagram shows the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) of Meridia. (a) Calculate Meridia’s inflation rate in 2024. [2] (b) Calculate Meridia’s inflation rate in 2025. [2] (c) A student says, “Prices fell in Meridia in 2025.” Explain whether the diagram supports this statement. [2]

Answer (inflation rate = change in CPI ÷ CPI in the earlier year × 100):

(a) Change in CPI = 114.4 − 104 = 10.4 (1). Inflation rate = 10.4 ÷ 104 × 100 = 10% (1).

(b) Change in CPI = 120.1 − 114.4 = 5.7 (1). Inflation rate = 5.7 ÷ 114.4 × 100 = 4.98%, which is 5.0% to one decimal place (1).

(c) No. The CPI rose from 114.4 to 120.1 in 2025, so the general price level was still rising (1). It was the inflation rate that fell, from 10% to about 5%: prices rose more slowly than in 2024, but they did not fall (1).

Examiner Tip
Read the slope of a CPI graph. A line that climbs means inflation; a line that climbs less steeply means a lower inflation rate; only a line that slopes down means falling prices (deflation). In part (b), divide by the CPI of the year before (114.4), not by the base-year value of 100: dividing by 100 gives 5.7%, which is wrong.

Example 9: Real GDP per head and the HDI

Practice question · Topic 5.1 · [6 marks]

The diagram shows the real GDP and the population of two countries, Norland and Sutara. The table gives more data for the same year. (a) Calculate the real GDP per head of each country. [2] (b) Explain two reasons why Sutara may have a higher Human Development Index (HDI) value than Norland. [4]

IndicatorNorlandSutara
HDI value0.700.78
Life expectancy at birth64 years76 years
Expected years of schooling10 years14 years

Answer:

(a) Real GDP per head = real GDP ÷ population.
Norland: $90 billion ÷ 6 million = $90,000 million ÷ 6 million = $15,000 (1).
Sutara: $240 billion ÷ 20 million = $240,000 million ÷ 20 million = $12,000 (1).

(b) The HDI measures health and education as well as income, so a country with a lower income per head can still have the higher HDI.
Reason 1: people in Sutara live longer, 76 years compared with 64 (1). Life expectancy is the health component of the HDI, so better healthcare, nutrition or sanitation in Sutara raises its HDI value (1).
Reason 2: children in Sutara can expect more schooling, 14 years compared with 10 (1). Years of schooling is the education component of the HDI, so this also raises Sutara’s HDI value (1).

Why this scores
Part (a) changes billions into millions before dividing, which is where most slips happen. The diagram shows the key point behind both parts: Sutara’s real GDP is about 2.7 times Norland’s, but its population is over 3 times as large, so its income per head is lower. Each reason then names an HDI component, quotes the data and links it to the HDI.

Example 10: Working out population change

Practice question · Topic 5.3 · [6 marks]

The diagram shows the birth rate, death rate and net migration rate of two countries for one year. Kalenga had a population of 40 million at the start of the year and Estovia had 50 million. (a) Calculate the change in Kalenga’s population during the year. [2] (b) Calculate the change in Estovia’s population during the year. [2] (c) Explain one reason why the birth rate may be higher in Kalenga than in Estovia. [2]

Answer (population change per 1,000 = birth rate − death rate + net migration rate):

(a) Kalenga: 32 − 9 − 3 = +20 per 1,000 (1). 40,000,000 × 20 ÷ 1,000 = a rise of 800,000 people (1).

(b) Estovia: 9 − 11 + 4 = +2 per 1,000 (1). 50,000,000 × 2 ÷ 1,000 = a rise of 100,000 people (1).

(c) One reason is that fewer women in Kalenga may stay in education and take up careers (1), so they tend to marry and have children earlier and have larger families (1). Other answers that would earn the marks: less access to contraception and family planning; children being needed to work and to support parents in old age where there is no state pension; a higher infant death rate, so parents have more children.

Examiner Tip
Look at the direction of each bar. Kalenga’s net migration bar points down: more people emigrated than immigrated, so you subtract. Estovia’s death rate is higher than its birth rate, so without migration its population would fall by 2 per 1,000; it grows only because of net immigration. A 20 per 1,000 change is the same as 2%, a quick check on your answer.

Example 11: An appreciation, drawn to scale

Practice question · Topic 6.3 · [6 marks]

Zentara has a floating exchange rate. Its currency is the zen (Z). Demand for Zentara’s exports rises, shifting the demand for the zen from D to D1 in the diagram. (a) Using the diagram, calculate the percentage appreciation of the zen. [2] (b) A bicycle made in Zentara is priced at Z500. Calculate its price in US$ before and after the appreciation. [2] (c) A pair of headphones imported into Zentara costs US$60. Calculate its price in zen before and after the appreciation. [2]

Answer:

(a) The price of the zen rises from US$0.40 to US$0.48 (1). Percentage appreciation = (0.48 − 0.40) ÷ 0.40 × 100 = 20% (1).

(b) Before: 500 × 0.40 = US$200 (1). After: 500 × 0.48 = US$240 (1). The export becomes more expensive for foreign buyers.

(c) Before: 60 ÷ 0.40 = Z150 (1). After: 60 ÷ 0.48 = Z125 (1). The import becomes cheaper for people in Zentara.

ItemAt Z1 = US$0.40At Z1 = US$0.48Effect of the appreciation
Z500 bicycle (export), price in US$US$200US$240Export price rises, so demand for exports is likely to fall
US$60 headphones (import), price in zenZ150Z125Import price falls, so demand for imports is likely to rise
Why this scores
The exchange rates are read from the diagram where D and D1 cross S, and each calculation goes the right way: to change zen into US$ you multiply by the price of the zen; to change US$ into zen you divide by it. To remember the effect of an appreciation, think “exports dearer, imports cheaper”. A depreciation does the opposite.

Example 12: Building the current account balance

Practice question · Topic 6.4 · [6 marks]

The diagram shows the money flowing into and out of Maravia for each of the four components of the current account of its balance of payments. (a) Calculate the balance on each of the four components. [4] (b) Calculate Maravia’s current account balance and state whether it is a deficit or a surplus. [2]

Answer (balance = money in − money out):

ComponentMoney in (US$bn)Money out (US$bn)Balance (US$bn)
Trade in goods120150120 − 150 = −30, a deficit (1)
Trade in services644264 − 42 = +22, a surplus (1)
Primary income183018 − 30 = −12, a deficit (1)
Secondary income14614 − 6 = +8, a surplus (1)

(b) Current account balance = −30 + 22 − 12 + 8 = −12 (1), a current account deficit of US$12 billion (1).

In the diagram, a component is in deficit wherever the “money out” bar is the taller of the pair (goods and primary income) and in surplus wherever the “money in” bar is taller (services and secondary income).

Examiner Tip
Keep the signs all the way through: add the four balances with their plus and minus signs, and only then decide whether the total is a deficit or a surplus. A country can have a surplus on trade in services and still have a current account deficit, as Maravia does. If a question asks only for the balance of trade in goods and services, stop after the first two rows: −30 + 22 = −US$8 billion.
Model Answers · Topic 1

Model Answers: The Basic Economic Problem

Full-mark model answers to past Paper 2 questions on scarcity, the factors of production, opportunity cost and the PPC. Use them to see how much detail each command word needs and how a chain of reasoning is built.

Define [2]

0455/22/F/M/22 (a) · [2 marks]

Define the economic problem.

The economic problem (called the basic economic problem in the 2027–2029 syllabus) is the situation in which there are unlimited wants but only limited (finite) resources to satisfy them, which creates scarcity and means choices have to be made.

Why this scores
One mark for unlimited wants and one for limited or scarce resources. Mentioning the need to make choices shows understanding but the two key ideas are what secure the marks.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
0455/22/O/N/23 (a) · [2 marks]

Define, with an example, a capital good.

A capital good is a human-made (man-made) good that is used to produce other goods and services, rather than being consumed for its own sake. For example, a delivery van used by a bakery or a tractor used on a farm.

Why this scores
One mark for a precise definition (human-made good used in production) and one for a valid example. Avoid money or shares as examples: they are financial capital, not capital goods.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Explain [4]

0455/22/O/N/22 (c) · [4 marks]

Explain the economic problem and why it is always likely to exist.

The economic problem is that people’s wants are unlimited, while the resources available to satisfy them (land, labour, capital and enterprise) are limited. This creates scarcity, so societies must decide what to produce, how to produce it and who to produce for.

It is always likely to exist because human wants keep growing: as incomes rise and new products are invented, people want more and better goods and services, such as newer phones or foreign holidays. At the same time, resources remain finite, and some, such as oil and minerals, are non-renewable and are being used up. Even if an economy grows, wants grow too, so there will never be enough resources to satisfy all wants and choices will always have to be made.

Why this scores
Two marks for explaining the problem (unlimited wants, limited resources, scarcity) and two for explaining why it persists (wants continually increase; resources remain finite or run out).
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
0455/21/M/J/25 (b) · [4 marks]

Explain two causes of a decrease in enterprise in an economy.

First, higher taxes on profits (corporation tax) reduce the reward for risk-taking. If entrepreneurs keep a smaller share of any profit they make, fewer people will think it worth risking their savings to start or expand a business, so the amount of enterprise falls.

Second, a recession or economic uncertainty makes it more likely that new businesses will fail. When demand is falling and the future is unclear, potential entrepreneurs expect lower sales and profits, and banks become less willing to lend to them, so fewer new firms are set up.

Why this scores
Each cause is identified (1) and then developed by linking it to the reward from, or risk of, enterprise (1). Two developed causes give 4 marks. The question asks for two, so a third cause would earn nothing: spend the time developing the two you have chosen.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
0455/22/M/J/23 (c) · [4 marks]

Explain one reason why the quantity of land may increase and one reason why the quality of land may increase.

Quantity: land reclamation, such as draining marshland or reclaiming land from the sea, creates new usable land. This adds to the total area that can be farmed or built on, so more land is available for production.

Quality: the use of fertilisers, irrigation and better farming techniques can make existing soil more productive, so each hectare of land yields a larger output.

Why this scores
One mark for each reason identified and one for each explanation of how it increases the amount or productivity of land. Keeping quantity and quality clearly separate avoids confusion. Other valid reasons: discovery of new natural resources (quantity); reducing pollution or reversing soil erosion (quality).
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
0455/22/F/M/20 (b) · [4 marks]

Explain how opportunity cost is different for economic goods and free goods.

Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. An economic good is produced using scarce resources, so producing or buying it has an opportunity cost: the resources used to make a car could have been used to make something else, and the money a consumer spends on it could have bought another product.

A free good, such as air or sunlight, is not scarce: it is available in unlimited quantity and needs no resources to produce. Using more of it does not mean giving anything else up, so a free good has zero opportunity cost.

Why this scores
Marks for defining or applying opportunity cost, explaining that economic goods use scarce resources so have an opportunity cost, and explaining that free goods are not scarce so have none.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
0455/22/F/M/21 (b) · [4 marks]

Explain the difference between a point inside a PPC and a point outside a PPC.

A point inside a PPC shows that the economy is not using all of its resources, or not using them efficiently. There is spare capacity, such as unemployed workers or idle machinery, so output could be increased without giving up any of the other good.

A point outside a PPC shows a combination of goods that the economy cannot currently produce with its existing resources and technology. It is unattainable at present and could only be reached if the PPC shifted outwards, through more or better-quality resources.

Why this scores
Two marks for inside (unemployed or inefficiently used resources) and two for outside (unattainable with current resources; needs economic growth).
Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Analyse [6]

0455/22/O/N/23 (c) · [6 marks]

Analyse, using a production possibility curve (PPC) diagram, the effect of a decrease in the size of a country’s labour force on its economy.

Labour is a factor of production, so a fall in the size of the labour force, for example because of emigration or an ageing population, reduces the quantity of resources available to the economy. With fewer workers, the maximum output the country can produce of both capital goods and consumer goods falls. This is shown by the PPC shifting inwards from PPC to PPC1, and the economy moving from a point such as A to B.

This means the country’s productive capacity has fallen, so its potential output is lower. Combinations that were previously attainable, such as A, are now outside the new curve. Fewer goods and services can be produced, which may reduce living standards unless output per worker rises. Firms may face labour shortages, which push up wage costs and prices, and the government may receive less income tax revenue while facing continued spending demands. The economy may also have to import more to meet domestic demand, worsening the current account of its balance of payments.

Why this scores
A correctly labelled diagram with an inward shift, a clear link from fewer workers to fewer factors of production to lower maximum output, and developed consequences (lower productive capacity, living standards, costs) earn all six marks. Analyse answers are point-marked: each correct diagram feature and each developed link in the chain earns a mark.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
0455/22/F/M/20 (c) · [6 marks]

Analyse, using a production possibility curve (PPC) diagram, the effect of an increase in enterprise on an economy.

Enterprise is the factor of production that organises land, labour and capital and takes the risks of production. An increase in enterprise means more people are willing to set up and run businesses. New firms bring previously idle resources into use and combine factors in new, more efficient ways, and entrepreneurs often introduce new products and technology. This increases both the quantity and the productivity of resources used, so the economy’s productive capacity rises. The PPC shifts outwards from PPC to PPC1, allowing a move from A to B, where more of both capital and consumer goods can be produced.

As a result, the economy experiences economic growth. Higher output creates more jobs, so unemployment may fall, and higher incomes can raise living standards. Competition from new firms can also lower prices and improve quality for consumers, and the government gains more tax revenue from higher profits and incomes, which it can spend on education or healthcare. Innovative firms may also sell abroad, increasing exports.

Why this scores
The answer defines the role of enterprise, links it to more and better use of resources, shows an outward PPC shift that is labelled and referred to, and develops outcomes (growth, jobs, living standards, tax revenue).
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
0455/23/M/J/20 (c) · [6 marks]

Analyse the influences on the mobility of two factors of production.

Backgroundnot required by the 2027–2029 syllabus in this form. Mobility of land, capital and enterprise has been removed; only the mobility of labour remains (Topic 3, 3.3.4). The labour paragraph is still useful; the capital paragraph is for past-paper practice only.

Labour can be geographically and occupationally mobile. Its geographical mobility (moving between places) is influenced by differences in the cost of housing, family and social ties, and access to information about jobs elsewhere. If housing in the area with vacancies is much more expensive, a worker may be unable to move there, so unemployment in one region can exist alongside labour shortages in another. Its occupational mobility (moving between jobs) depends on skills, qualifications and training. A coal miner who loses their job may lack the skills to become a software engineer, and so stays unemployed without retraining. Government training schemes and better education therefore increase labour mobility and help resources move to where they are most needed.

Capital mobility depends on the type of capital. Some capital is occupationally mobile: a computer or a delivery van can be used in many different industries. Other capital is specialised, such as a car-assembly robot or an oil rig, and cannot easily be switched to other uses, so it has low occupational mobility. Geographical mobility is also influenced by size and weight: laptops can be moved easily, while factories, dams and railway lines are fixed in one place. When capital is immobile, it may stand idle if demand for what it produces falls, leaving the economy producing inside its PPC.

Why this scores
Two factors are clearly identified, each with influences on both geographical and occupational mobility, and the answer analyses the consequence (unemployment, idle resources, inefficiency) rather than just listing influences.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Discuss [8]

0455/22/M/J/20 (d) · [8 marks]

Discuss whether or not an ageing population is a benefit to an economy.

Why it may be a benefit. An ageing population means older people form a rising proportion of the population. Older workers often have valuable experience and skills. If they stay in work for longer, their experience can raise productivity and help train younger workers, increasing the quality of the labour force. Also, many older people have built up savings and pensions and spend them on goods and services such as healthcare, travel and leisure. This creates demand for new industries (sometimes called the “silver economy”), which encourages firms to invest and creates jobs. In addition, retired people often care for grandchildren or volunteer, freeing younger family members to work.

Why it may not be a benefit. An ageing population usually means a smaller share of people are of working age, so the dependency ratio rises. Fewer workers must support more dependants, so the labour force may shrink, causing labour shortages that push up wage costs and reduce the economy’s productive capacity, shifting the PPC inwards. Furthermore, the government must spend more on state pensions and healthcare while receiving less income tax from a smaller workforce. This creates pressure to raise taxes, cut other spending such as education or infrastructure, or borrow more, which may reduce incentives to work and harm future economic growth. Older workers may also be less occupationally mobile and less willing to retrain in new technologies.

Conclusion. An ageing population is more likely to be a burden than a benefit if it causes the labour force to shrink quickly while pension and health costs rise. However, it depends on how the economy responds: if the retirement age is raised, older people stay healthy and productive, immigration adds working-age people, and firms adopt labour-saving technology, the costs can be managed and the spending of older people can even boost demand. It also depends on the speed of ageing, since a gradual change gives the government time to plan.

Why this scores
Two developed arguments on each side (experience, new demand; dependency ratio, government finances) and a conclusion that makes a judgement and states what it depends on (retirement age, immigration, technology, speed of change).
Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Quick Checklist

  • In my answer I used precise definitions with the key words (unlimited wants, limited resources, human-made, next best alternative).
  • In my answer I developed each point with “which means that” rather than listing.
  • In my answer I drew the PPC concave to the origin, labelled both axes, PPC and PPC1, and showed the shift with an arrow.
  • In my answer I referred to my diagram in the writing and explained why the curve shifted.
  • In my answer I linked changes in factors of production to productive capacity, output and living standards.
  • In my answer I gave both sides of a Discuss question and finished with a justified “it depends on” conclusion.
Model Answers · Topics 2–3

Model Answers: Markets, Firms & Workers

Full-mark model answers to typical Paper 2 questions on demand and supply, price elasticity, productivity, labour markets, monopoly and firms’ objectives. Use them to see how a precise definition, a developed explanation, a chain of analysis and a balanced discussion each earn their marks.

State / Define [2]

Past paper (a) · [2 marks]

State the formula used to calculate PED.

PED = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.

Why this scores
One mark for “percentage change in quantity demanded” on top and one for “percentage change in price” underneath. Writing “change in demand” or dropping the word “percentage” loses marks, as does putting the terms the wrong way up.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Explain [4]

Past paper (b) · [4 marks]

Explain two reasons why the price of sugar may fall.

Increase in supply. A good harvest, caused by favourable weather or better fertilisers, raises the quantity of sugar cane produced at every price. The supply curve shifts to the right, so at the old price there is a surplus of sugar. Sellers cut the price to clear the excess stock, so the equilibrium price falls.

Decrease in demand. Health campaigns warning about obesity and diabetes change tastes away from sugary products, so households and food and drink producers buy less sugar. Demand for sugar falls at every price, shifting the demand curve to the left. This creates a surplus at the original price, and competition between sellers pushes the price down.

Why this scores
Two separate causes (one supply-side, one demand-side), each identified and then developed by explaining the shift and how the resulting surplus lowers price.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (b) · [4 marks]

Explain two causes of a shift to the right in the demand curve for fish.

A rise in the price of a substitute such as meat. If beef and chicken become more expensive, fish becomes relatively cheaper. Some consumers switch from meat to fish, so more fish is demanded at every price and the demand curve shifts right.

A change in tastes in favour of fish. If reports show that eating oily fish is good for heart health, or consumers switch away from meat for environmental reasons, fish becomes more desirable. People are willing and able to buy more fish at each price, so demand increases and the curve shifts right.

(Other creditworthy causes: a rise in incomes, as fish is a normal good; a fall in the price of a complement such as rice or chips; a rise in population; successful advertising.)

Why this scores
Each cause is a non-price determinant of demand (a change in price would cause a movement along the curve, not a shift) and each is explained in terms of more being demanded at every price.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (b) · [4 marks]

Explain what effect more firms producing tyres would have on the PED of individual firms’ tyres.

More firms producing tyres would make the demand for each individual firm’s tyres more price elastic. With more producers, consumers have a greater number of close substitutes to choose from. If one firm raises its price, buyers can easily switch to a rival’s similar tyres, so the firm would lose a large proportion of its sales. A given percentage rise in price would now cause a larger percentage fall in quantity demanded than before, so the PED figure becomes larger (further from zero) and, with enough close substitutes, greater than 1. As a result, each firm has less power to raise prices and would be under pressure to keep prices low or to differentiate its tyres through branding or quality.

Why this scores
States the direction of change (more elastic), gives the reason (more substitutes), develops it (consumers switch, large fall in quantity demanded) and links it to the size of the PED figure and the firm’s pricing power.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (b) · [4 marks]

Explain how market forces will eliminate a surplus and a shortage.

Surplus. A surplus occurs when the price is above equilibrium, so quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. Sellers are left with unsold stock, so they lower their price. As the price falls, quantity demanded extends and quantity supplied contracts until the two are equal at the equilibrium price and the surplus disappears.

Shortage. A shortage occurs when the price is below equilibrium, so quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. Consumers compete for the limited goods and sellers realise they can charge more, so the price rises. The higher price causes quantity demanded to contract and quantity supplied to extend until the market clears at equilibrium.

Why this scores
Defines each disequilibrium, explains the price movement and uses “extension” and “contraction” correctly to show how equilibrium is restored without government intervention.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (b) · [4 marks]

Explain two ways a firm could increase the productivity of its workers.

Training. The firm could provide on-the-job or off-the-job training. This improves workers’ skills and knowledge, so they work faster, make fewer mistakes and can operate more advanced equipment. Output per worker per hour therefore rises.

Investing in better capital. The firm could buy more advanced machinery or technology, such as automated production lines or faster computers. Each worker then has more and better capital to work with, which allows them to produce more output in the same time, raising labour productivity.

(Other valid ways: incentive schemes such as piece rates or bonuses, improving working conditions and motivation, better management and organisation of tasks through division of labour.)

Why this scores
Two distinct methods, each linked explicitly to higher output per worker, which is the definition of labour productivity.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Analyse [6]

Past paper (c) · [6 marks]

Analyse, using a demand and supply diagram, the effect of an increase in demand for cars on the market for tyres.

Cars and tyres are complements (joint demand): every new car needs tyres, and more cars on the road means more replacement tyres are needed. So an increase in demand for cars leads to an increase in demand for tyres at every price.

In the diagram the demand curve for tyres shifts to the right from D to D1. At the original price P there is now a shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Tyre buyers (car manufacturers and motorists) compete for the limited supply, pushing the price up. The higher price gives tyre producers an incentive to produce more, so quantity supplied extends along the supply curve S. A new equilibrium is reached where D1 crosses S, at a higher price P1 and a higher quantity Q1.

As a result, tyre producers’ revenue rises (both price and quantity sold increase), which may raise their profits, attract new firms into the industry and increase demand for the rubber and labour used to make tyres. The size of the price rise depends on the PES of tyres: if supply is elastic, most of the effect is on quantity rather than price.

Why this scores
A fully labelled diagram (axes, S, D, D1, P, P1, Q, Q1), the link between the markets (complements/joint demand), the correct shift, the adjustment process via the shortage, and the outcome with a consequence for firms.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (c) · [6 marks]

Analyse why an actor may decide to become a teacher.

Workers choose an occupation by weighing up its wage and non-wage factors.

Wage factors. Most actors earn low and irregular incomes: they are paid per role and may spend long periods with no work. There is a large supply of people wanting to act relative to demand, which keeps the typical wage low. Teachers, by contrast, usually receive a regular salary on a pay scale, often with annual increments and a pension. An actor who wants a higher and more predictable income may therefore switch to teaching, because the expected lifetime earnings are greater and allow them to plan borrowing, such as a mortgage.

Non-wage factors. Teaching offers greater job security, since there is continuous demand for teachers and posts are often permanent contracts, whereas acting jobs are temporary. Teachers usually have long holidays and regular hours rather than evening and weekend performances and touring away from home, which can suit someone with a family. Teaching can also offer job satisfaction from helping young people and clear promotion prospects, for example to head of department.

Transferable skills. An actor already has skills in communication, confidence and presenting to an audience, so the cost of retraining (for example, a teaching qualification) may be relatively low, making the move easier. Occupational mobility is higher when skills overlap. Overall, if the combined wage and non-wage benefits of teaching exceed those of acting, the actor will change occupation.

Why this scores
Uses the economic framework of wage and non-wage factors, compares both jobs rather than describing one, and develops each point into why it would change the actor’s choice, with a link to occupational mobility.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Discuss [8]

Past paper (d) · [8 marks]

Discuss whether or not demand for coffee is likely to rise in the future.

Why demand may rise.

Incomes are rising in many developing and emerging economies, such as China and India. Coffee, especially café coffee, is a normal good, so as real incomes grow consumers can afford to buy more of it at every price. The demand curve shifts to the right.

Tastes are also changing. Coffee-shop culture is spreading, and advertising by large chains and social media promotes coffee as a lifestyle product. Population growth in countries with a young, urban population also adds more potential consumers. Both increase the number of people willing and able to buy coffee.

Why demand may not rise.

Health concerns about too much caffeine could shift tastes towards substitutes such as herbal tea, fruit juice or water, reducing demand for coffee. If the price of a close substitute such as tea falls, some consumers will switch away from coffee.

Climate change may reduce the supply of coffee beans, as coffee plants are sensitive to rising temperatures and droughts. This would raise the price of coffee, causing a contraction in quantity demanded (a movement along the curve). A recession would also reduce incomes and cut spending on non-essential purchases such as café coffee.

Conclusion. Demand for coffee is likely to rise overall, because the growth in incomes and population in emerging economies is a long-term trend that outweighs health concerns in most markets. However, it depends on the country: in high-income countries where consumption is already high, demand may be stable or fall as tastes shift, and it also depends on whether a future recession cuts incomes.

Why this scores
Two developed arguments on each side using determinants of demand, a clear distinction between a shift in demand and a contraction caused by a price rise, and a conclusion that makes a judgement and says what it depends on.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (d) · [8 marks]

Discuss whether or not skilled workers are always paid more than unskilled workers.

Why skilled workers are usually paid more.

The supply of skilled workers is limited. Skills such as those of surgeons or engineers take years of education and training to acquire and require particular abilities, so few people can do the job. The supply of labour is low and inelastic, which pushes the wage up.

Skilled workers also tend to have high productivity: they produce more output, or output of greater value, per hour. Firms’ demand for labour is a derived demand, so they are willing to pay a high wage to workers who add a lot of revenue. High demand combined with low supply gives a high equilibrium wage.

Why skilled workers are not always paid more.

Demand for some skills can be low or falling. A skilled craftworker in a declining industry, or a worker whose skill has been replaced by automation, may earn less than an unskilled worker in a booming sector, because the derived demand for their labour has fallen.

Wages also depend on bargaining power and government. Unskilled workers in an industry with a strong trade union may win higher pay than non-unionised skilled workers, and a national minimum wage can raise unskilled pay. In some public-sector jobs, such as nursing or teaching, skilled workers are paid by government pay scales that may be lower than the wages of unskilled workers doing dangerous or unpleasant work, such as offshore oil labourers who receive compensation for poor conditions. Some skilled workers also accept lower pay for non-wage benefits, such as job satisfaction.

Conclusion. Skilled workers are usually, but not always, paid more. It depends on the demand for the skill relative to its supply: a skill that is in short supply and highly valued by employers earns a high wage, but where demand for a skill is low, or unskilled workers have strong unions, dangerous conditions or minimum wage protection, the gap can narrow or reverse.

Why this scores
Uses demand and supply of labour on both sides, brings in trade unions, government policy, extra pay for dangerous or unpleasant work and non-wage factors, and the word “always” is directly challenged in a reasoned conclusion.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (d) · [8 marks]

Discuss whether all monopolies have low costs of production.

Why monopolies may have low costs.

A monopoly is the only firm supplying its market, so it usually produces on a very large scale. This allows it to benefit from economies of scale: for example, bulk-buying discounts on raw materials (purchasing economies), cheaper borrowing because lenders see it as low risk (financial economies) and the use of specialist, efficient machinery (technical economies). Average total cost (ATC) falls as output rises.

A monopoly can also keep earning high profits because barriers to entry stop new firms entering the market. It can use these profits to fund research and development, leading to new, more efficient production methods that cut costs further. In industries with very high fixed costs, such as a water supply network, one firm supplying the whole market can spread those costs over the largest possible output, giving a lower average total cost than several small firms could achieve.

Why monopolies may not have low costs.

Without competition, a monopoly has little incentive to keep costs down. It can survive while being inefficient, for example by overstaffing, paying managers high salaries or using out-of-date equipment, because customers have no alternative supplier. Rising costs can simply be passed on as higher prices.

A monopoly may also grow so large that it suffers diseconomies of scale: communication becomes slower, management becomes harder to coordinate and workers feel less motivated, so average costs rise. In addition, a monopoly in a small local market (such as the only shop on an island) may not be large enough to gain significant economies of scale at all.

Conclusion. Not all monopolies have low costs. It depends on their size and on whether they face pressure to be efficient: a large monopoly that reinvests profits and faces the threat of regulation or potential competitors is likely to have low costs, whereas a protected monopoly with no competitive pressure, or one that has grown too large, may have high costs.

Why this scores
Names specific economies and diseconomies of scale, uses monopoly concepts (barriers to entry, high profits, lack of competition) and gives a conclusion that directly answers “all”.
Written your own answer? Get it marked →
Past paper (d) · [8 marks]

Discuss whether or not a firm should have growth as its main objective.

Why growth should be the main objective.
